sources.citation: B. Beyer, C. Jones, J. Petoff, and N. R. Murphy, Eds., Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems, ch. 6, "Monitoring Distributed Systems" (R. Ewaschuk). Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, 2016. [Online]. Available: https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/
sources.paper_claim: Contribution 3 and Abstract: the rate-limiting arm 'establish[es] that no latency statistic is interpretable without an error-rate denominator'; also Discussion 6.3.
sources.what_it_says: The Four Golden Signals section states that "It's important to distinguish between the latency of successful requests and the latency of failed requests," warns that an HTTP 500 "triggered due to loss of connection to a database or other critical backend might be served very quickly" so that "factoring 500s into your overall latency might result in misleading calculations," and adds that "a slow error is even worse than a fast error!" It further prescribes errors as a first-class signal to be reported alongside latency. The paper's Arm B is this exact hazard, with 429 substituted for 500.
sources.why_it_matters: This is the strongest prior-art conflict in the audit. The paper cites this very book (ref [3]) but only Ch. 4 on percentiles, and its Related Work never mentions the golden signals. The result therefore cannot be claimed as establishing the principle; it can only be claimed as quantifying it. Fix: add this to Section 2 and downgrade Contribution 3 from 'establishing' to 'quantifying under controlled ablation'.

sources.citation: S. Thurgood and D. Ferguson, with A. Hidalgo and B. Beyer, "Implementing SLOs," ch. 2 in The Site Reliability Workbook: Practical Ways to Implement SRE, B. Beyer, N. R. Murphy, D. K. Rensin, K. Kawahara, and S. Thorne, Eds. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, 2018. [Online]. Available: https://sre.google/workbook/implementing-slos/
sources.paper_claim: Section 6.4 implication 1: 'Report mean and a high percentile and an error rate. Any one alone is defeasible.' Also Section 5.6's p99-SLO argument.
sources.what_it_says: Defines the availability SLI as "The proportion of requests that resulted in a successful response" and the latency SLI as "The proportion of requests that were faster than some threshold" — i.e. the standard latency SLI is already a ratio over valid requests, not a percentile of served latencies, and is specified alongside an availability SLI rather than instead of one. Caveat: the fetched page rendered the containing book's title oddly (as a site heading rather than 'The Site Reliability Workbook'); chapter title, chapter authors, publisher and year were confirmed on the page, and the book identity is that of sre.google/workbook.
sources.why_it_matters: The paper's headline practice recommendation is already the industry-standard SLI specification. More usefully for the paper, the 'proportion faster than a threshold' form is structurally immune to both failure modes the paper identifies — the Arm B artefact (a 429 is not a fast success) and the Section 5.6 incidence blindness (a 0.1% slow path moves a proportion-based SLI even though it cannot move p99). This is a concrete, citable remedy the paper's Discussion currently lacks.

sources.citation: T. Hauer, P. Hoffmann, J. Lunney, D. Ardelean, and A. Diwan, "Meaningful availability," in Proc. 17th USENIX Symp. Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI '20), Santa Clara, CA, Feb. 2020, pp. 545-557. [Online]. Available: https://research.google/pubs/pub50828/
sources.paper_claim: Section 6.3, that latency statistics 'describe only the requests that were served' and any regime lacking an error rate 'can be made to look arbitrarily good by a system that fails faster'.
sources.what_it_says: A Google production study arguing that standard availability metrics are misleading and must be replaced: time-based metrics (MTTR/MTTF) and count-based success ratio both fail to reflect user-perceived reliability. Proposes user-uptime, an event-based but time-sensitive metric, plus windowed uptime for aggregation, validated on a G Suite case study distinguishing brief flakiness from sustained outage.
sources.why_it_matters: This is the closest peer-reviewed analogue to the paper's argument and should be in Related Work. It shows the 'the denominator is the problem' critique is an established research line, not a new observation. It also cuts against the paper: it argues that even a plain success-ratio error rate — precisely the denominator the paper recommends adding — is itself misleading, because it over-weights heavy users and short outages. The paper's remedy is therefore weaker than the state of the art, which is a fair limitation to concede.

sources.citation: H. Zhou, M. Chen, Q. Lin, Y. Wang, X. She, S. Liu, R. Gu, B. C. Ooi, and J. Yang, "Overload control for scaling WeChat microservices," in Proc. ACM Symp. Cloud Computing (SoCC '18), Carlsbad, CA, Oct. 2018, pp. 149-161. doi: 10.1145/3267809.3267823. [Online]. Available: https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.04075
sources.paper_claim: Section 5.7 / H3: under load shedding, latency and throughput metrics improve while the service fails.
sources.what_it_says: Presents DAGOR, a load-shedding overload-control scheme in WeChat production for five years. The stated evaluation criterion is that "DAGOR can benefit high success rate of service even when the system is experiencing overload, while ensuring fairness in the overload control" — success rate, not latency, is the metric by which a load-shedding system is judged.
sources.why_it_matters: Independent confirmation from a large production system that latency is not the operative metric once shedding engages: the systems community already evaluates load shedders on success rate for exactly the reason the paper discovers. Supports the finding while confirming it is established practice. Also a useful citation for the paper's own framing in 5.7 that 'the limiter itself is not defective'.

sources.citation: M. Ulrich, "Addressing Cascading Failures," ch. 22 in Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems, B. Beyer, C. Jones, J. Petoff, and N. R. Murphy, Eds. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, 2016. [Online]. Available: https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/
sources.paper_claim: Section 5.7's mechanism explanation: 'A rejection really is cheaper to produce than a search... The server got fast by stopping the work it exists to do.'
sources.what_it_says: On load shedding under overload, instructs that servers "should protect themselves from becoming overloaded and crashing. When overloaded at either the frontend or backend layers, fail early and cheaply," giving as a straightforward implementation returning HTTP 503 once in-flight requests exceed a threshold, and advising operators to "Monitor and alert when too many servers enter these modes."
sources.why_it_matters: "Fail early and cheaply" is the designed-in mechanism behind the paper's 52.8x measured speedup — the cheapness is a deliberate property of correct load shedders, not an incidental artefact of this application's rate limiter. Citing it strengthens the paper's generalisation claim (the artefact should reproduce on any correctly built shedder) while further confirming the mechanism was already understood.

sources.citation: C. Klein, M. Maggio, K.-E. Arzen, and F. Hernandez-Rodriguez, "Brownout: building more robust cloud applications," in Proc. 36th Int. Conf. Software Engineering (ICSE 2014), Hyderabad, India, May 2014, pp. 700-711. doi: 10.1145/2568225.2568227. [Online]. Available: https://portal.research.lu.se/en/publications/brownout-building-more-robust-cloud-applications
sources.paper_claim: Section 6.3's general claim that latency reporting 'can be made to look arbitrarily good by a system that fails faster'.
sources.what_it_says: Introduces brownout, a self-adaptation paradigm in which applications mark parts of their response as optional code that a control loop dynamically deactivates under load, so that response time is held to target without over-provisioning. Evaluated on RUBiS and RUBBoS with under 170 lines of change, improving resilience to flash crowds and hardware failure.
sources.why_it_matters: Generalises the paper's finding past the binary success/error case, and this is the version the paper's error-rate remedy does not cover. Under brownout the requests all return HTTP 200 and latency is held at target by deliberately serving less content, so an error-rate denominator detects nothing. Worth one sentence in Discussion 6.3 or Future Work: the honest boundary of the paper's recommendation is that it catches fast failure, not degraded success. Note: DOI taken from the ACM DL identifier; title, authors, venue and year confirmed on the fetched Lund University portal record.

sources.citation: J. Li, N. K. Sharma, D. R. K. Ports, and S. D. Gribble, "Tales of the tail: Hardware, OS, and application-level sources of tail latency," in Proc. ACM Symp. Cloud Computing (SoCC '14), Seattle, WA, Nov. 2014. doi: 10.1145/2670979.2670988.
sources.paper_claim: Section 2, "Tail latency" paragraph (currently grounded only on Dean & Barroso [2]); and Section 5.1's claim that "the queue is forming inside the application, not in the load generator."
sources.what_it_says: Measures a null RPC service, Memcached and Nginx on single multi-core Linux hosts and models each as a queueing system to establish the best achievable latency distribution, then shows measured tails are far worse than the model predicts until specific causes are removed: background process interference, request scheduling discipline, interrupt routing, CPU power-management states and NUMA effects. Optimised Memcached on four cores at 80% utilisation reached 11 us median and 32 us p99.9, against 100 us / 5 ms for the unoptimised single-core case.
sources.why_it_matters: Dean & Barroso is a fan-out-across-many-machines argument; this study is one Node.js process on one host, so a reviewer will immediately ask why the only tail-latency citation is about a regime the paper does not test. Li et al. is the standard peer-reviewed single-node tail-latency reference and closes that gap. It also supplies a queueing-model baseline that Section 5.1's p99/p50 sweep could be compared against rather than described qualitatively, and it independently justifies the Section 7 concern about background desktop load and the balanced power profile, since it shows power states and scheduling shift tails specifically rather than uniformly.

sources.citation: J. C. Mogul and J. Wilkes, "Nines are not enough: Meaningful metrics for clouds," in Proc. 17th Workshop on Hot Topics in Operating Systems (HotOS '19), Bertinoro, Italy, May 2019.
sources.paper_claim: Contribution 3 and Section 6.3, "No latency statistic survives without an error rate"; also the Section 6.4 recommendation to report mean, a high percentile and an error rate together.
sources.what_it_says: Argues that the guarantees cloud providers actually offer are not meaningful to customers, that expressing SLOs in "nines" hides the difference between many short outages and a few long ones and treats all failures as equally costly, and that the problem resembles making decisions from sampled data. Offers a partial framework for reasoning about SLOs and lists the unsolved parts.
sources.why_it_matters: Section 5.7 is the paper's strongest and least expected result, and it is currently defended entirely by the study's own data plus the SRE book. This is the peer-reviewed precedent for the same structural point: the summary statistic is the wrong object, not merely badly computed. It converts "we found something surprising" into "we produce controlled evidence for a critique the SLO literature has already made on other grounds," which is a much stronger framing for Section 6.3 and for the practice recommendations in 6.4.

sources.citation: H. Kasture and D. Sanchez, "TailBench: A benchmark suite and evaluation methodology for latency-critical applications," in Proc. 2016 IEEE Int. Symp. Workload Characterization (IISWC), Providence, RI, Sep. 2016.
sources.paper_claim: Section 4 methodology as a whole, Section 5.8's coordinated-omission control, and the Section 7 "Shared host" threat to validity arising from the loopback 127.0.0.1 setup.
sources.what_it_says: Presents eight latency-critical benchmarks plus a harness implementing what the authors call a robust, statistically sound load-testing methodology, measuring both the service and the queueing components of request latency. The introduction states that widely used load testers suffer methodological pitfalls that cause orders-of-magnitude measurement errors. The harness supports networked, loopback and integrated configurations, and the authors report validation showing the simplified single-node configurations are accurate for most applications.
sources.why_it_matters: Two distinct gaps. First, coordinated omission is currently cited only to a conference talk [4] and vendor documentation [5]; Schroeder et al. [6] is peer-reviewed but is about open versus closed models generally, not about latency instrumentation. TailBench is the peer-reviewed methodology citation for measuring queueing delay rather than service time alone. Second, and more useful to this specific paper, its validation of loopback and same-host configurations against networked ones is direct published support for the Section 4.1 environment that Section 7 concedes as a weakness. That turns a conceded threat into a defended design choice.

sources.citation: Y. Zhang, D. Meisner, J. Mars, and L. Tang, "Treadmill: Attributing the source of tail latency through precise load testing and statistical inference," in Proc. 43rd ACM/IEEE Int. Symp. Computer Architecture (ISCA '16), Jun. 2016.
sources.paper_claim: Section 4.3, "Statistical treatment" (currently supported by Georges et al. [9] and Hoefler & Belli [10]); Section 5.4's demonstration that Mann-Whitney p = 0 at r = 0.0417 is uninformative; and Section 5.9 on percentile aggregation.
sources.what_it_says: Identifies three named deficiencies in existing tail-latency evaluation: poor load tester design, statistically inaccurate aggregation, and improper attribution of effects. Presents the Treadmill load tester and a statistically rigorous evaluation methodology, and extends quantile regression to attribute tail-latency effects to specific hardware features on Facebook production workloads, reporting a 43% p99 reduction and 93% variance reduction from the resulting tuning.
sources.why_it_matters: Georges et al. is about Java benchmarking and Hoefler & Belli about HPC; neither is about latency tails, so a reviewer in this area will expect the tail-latency-specific rigour paper. Its "statistically inaccurate aggregation" complaint is the same phenomenon Section 5.9 measures as raw-versus-time-quantized percentile bias, giving that section a citable precedent it currently lacks. Its use of quantile regression also pre-empts the obvious methodological objection to Section 5.4: Mann-Whitney tests the whole distribution, whereas the paper's claims are about specific quantiles, and quantile regression is the standard tool for testing a hypothesis at p99 directly.

sources.citation: C. Masson, J. E. Rim, and H. K. Lee, "DDSketch: A fast and fully-mergeable quantile sketch with relative-error guarantees," Proc. VLDB Endowment, vol. 12, no. 12, pp. 2195-2205, Aug. 2019. doi: 10.14778/3352063.3352135.
sources.paper_claim: Section 4.3, "Time-quantized percentiles," and Section 5.9's conclusion that "a percentile is therefore not one well-defined quantity." Also bears on Section 4.2's decision to retain the full per-request series.
sources.what_it_says: Motivates from web-application latency monitoring; its Figure 2 shows a real web endpoint whose mean latency sits closer to p75 than to p50. Notes that mean and variance are cheap to maintain over distributed streams but order statistics can only be approximately summarised, that rank-error guarantees do not preclude arbitrarily large relative errors on skewed data (which is common in practice), and that mergeability is a required property because several combined sketches must be as accurate as a single sketch of the same data.
sources.why_it_matters: Section 5.9 makes an unattributed claim that a percentile depends on the sampling unit. This is the peer-reviewed anchor for it, and for the stronger adjacent point the paper does not currently make: percentiles cannot be averaged or combined arithmetically at all, which is why sketch mergeability is a research problem. It also exposes an unstated advantage of the study's own method, since Section 4.2 keeps every request and computes exact percentiles while the production dashboards the paper criticises report sketch estimates carrying their own error, and the Datadog Figure 2 example is independent field evidence for the paper's central mean-versus-tail claim.

sources.citation: C. Delimitrou and C. Kozyrakis, "Amdahl's law for tail latency," Communications of the ACM, vol. 61, no. 8, pp. 65-72, Aug. 2018. doi: 10.1145/3232559.
sources.paper_claim: Section 5.1 and Section 6.2, "Percentiles matter most before a system looks broken" - the finding that p99/p50 peaks at 4 VUs (3.85) and falls to 1.17 at 200, described as "mechanically obvious in hindsight."
sources.what_it_says: Builds a queueing-theory model translating Amdahl's Law to tail latency. Argues that optimising for tail latency makes the serial fraction more consequential than optimising for average performance, and that the serial component determines not only whether throughput scales but how predictably the system responds under load. The banner line states that queueing-theoretic models can guide design trade-offs in systems targeting tail latency, not just average performance.
sources.why_it_matters: The paper's system is a textbook instance of this model: a single serialised stage (blocking JSON.parse on Node's one JavaScript thread) with throughput pinned at roughly 2,116 req/s, which is exactly the serial-fraction regime the article analyses. Citing it replaces "mechanically obvious in hindsight" with an analytical prediction. It also flags a question a reviewer is likely to raise, though this is my inference and not a claim made in the article: standard queueing results give a roughly constant tail-to-mean ratio under exponential service times, whereas Arm D reports p99/mean falling to 1.13, which implies near-deterministic service time. Whether the observed collapse is a general property of saturation or a property of this workload's low service-time variability is the boundary condition Section 8 leaves for future work, and the queueing model would let the paper settle it analytically.

sources.citation: R. Ewaschuk, "Monitoring Distributed Systems," ch. 6 in Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems, B. Beyer, C. Jones, J. Petoff, and N. R. Murphy, Eds. Sebastopol, CA: O'Reilly Media, 2016. [Online]. Available: https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/
sources.paper_claim: Contribution 3 (Sec. 1.2): the rate-limiting arm is claimed as 'establishing that no latency statistic is interpretable without an error-rate denominator'; restated in the Abstract and in Discussion 6.3 ('Latency statistics describe only the requests that were served').
sources.what_it_says: Independently re-fetched. The Four Golden Signals section states verbatim: "It's important to distinguish between the latency of successful requests and the latency of failed requests," warns that "an HTTP 500 error triggered due to loss of connection to a database or other critical backend might be served very quickly," and adds "a slow error is even worse than a fast error! Therefore, it's important to track error latency, as opposed to just filtering out errors." Errors are defined as a first-class signal: "The rate of requests that fail, either explicitly (e.g., HTTP 500s), implicitly ... or by policy." Confirmed on the page: ch. 6, author Rob Ewaschuk, O'Reilly Media (the online edition footer carries a 2017 copyright; the print first edition is 2016, which is the year the paper already uses for ref [3]).
sources.why_it_matters: The strongest finding in this audit. The paper's Arm B is precisely the hazard this chapter names — a cheap rejection served fast, with 429 substituted for 500 — and the chapter's 'errors, either explicitly ... or by policy' wording covers 429 rate-limit rejections directly. The paper cites this book as ref [3] but only ch. 4 on percentiles, and Sec. 2 (Related Work) contains no mention of the golden signals or of error rate as a signal; grep of the prose source confirms the words SLI, SLO, availability and load shedding appear nowhere in the literature review. Contribution 3 therefore cannot claim to establish the principle. Concrete fix: add a Related Work paragraph citing this chapter, and downgrade Contribution 3 from 'establishing' to 'quantifying, under controlled ablation, how far the two statistics can be driven apart from the truth (52.8x and 21.3x apparent improvement at 99.998% failure)'. Note this is the same book as ref [3] but a materially different chapter making a different claim, so it is not a duplicate citation — but the paper should cite it as a distinct chapter entry to make that visible.

sources.citation: T. Kalibera and R. E. Jones, "Rigorous benchmarking in reasonable time," in Proc. 2013 ACM SIGPLAN Int. Symp. Memory Management (ISMM '13), Seattle, WA, USA, Jun. 2013, pp. 63-74. doi: 10.1145/2464157.2464160.
sources.paper_claim: §4.5 "Each cell was repeated with the first run discarded as warm-up"; §7 Repeat counts ("Arm A used n = 4 per cell... Arm D n = 5 / n = 2... Arm B n = 6 / n = 2... Arm E n = 2"); §5.2, §5.5, §5.6, §5.7 tables, which report point estimates only.
sources.what_it_says: Repetition should be placed where the uncertainty actually is (between builds, between executions, between iterations), and the required number of repetitions at each level should be derived from a variance decomposition of pilot data to hit a stated precision target, rather than fixed by convention. It also argues results should be summarised as an effect size with a confidence interval, not as a bare point estimate.
sources.why_it_matters: This is the closest thing to a canonical answer for "is n = 4 to n = 6 enough?", and the answer it gives is that the question is unanswerable as posed: the count has to be justified from observed variance, and the summary has to carry an interval. The paper does neither. No table in §5 reports a standard deviation, a range, or a CI for any cell mean or percentile, yet §7 asserts "the effects reported are large relative to the observed spread" - the spread is claimed but never shown, so the reader cannot check the assertion. Under this standard the fix is cheap and does not need new runs: emit per-cell min/max or a CI from the runs already retained (facts.json already holds them), and state how n was chosen. The weakest cells by this criterion are the single-run Arm C percentile ladder (§5.6, the paper's only support for H4), Arm D ×1000 (n = 2), Arm B limiter-on (n = 2) and Arm E (n = 2, already flagged in the paper's own "Spread caution" note). The same source also bears on §4.3/§5.4: reporting rank-biserial r as a point value is better than reporting p alone, but the accepted form is r with an interval.

sources.citation: E. Barrett, C. F. Bolz-Tereick, R. Killick, S. Mount, and L. Tratt, "Virtual machine warmup blows hot and cold," Proc. ACM Program. Lang., vol. 1, no. OOPSLA, Oct. 2017. doi: 10.1145/3133876.
sources.paper_claim: §4.5 "Each cell was repeated with the first run discarded as warm-up"; §5.2 "9 warm-up runs discarded, n = 4 per cell"; §7 Repeat counts.
sources.what_it_says: Measurement methodology "almost always" discards data from an assumed warm-up phase and then treats the remainder as steady-state peak performance. Using automated changepoint analysis on JIT-compiled VMs under highly controlled conditions, the authors find at most 43.5% of (VM, benchmark) pairs consistently reach a steady state of peak performance; others never stabilise, stabilise at a slower rate than they started, or vary unpredictably between process executions.
sources.why_it_matters: The system under test is Node.js v24 on V8 - a JIT VM, squarely in scope for this result. "First run discarded" is exactly the fixed-rule warm-up heuristic this paper shows to be unsound; discarding by rule does not establish that the retained runs are in a steady state, and in a minority of cases no steady state exists to reach. The paper has strong evidence for one configuration and does not use it: the soak (§5.4, 3,599 s, degradation ratio 0.9944, flat per-quarter memory) is direct evidence that the knee configuration is stationary once warm. That argument should be made explicitly as the justification for the discard rule, with the scope limit stated - it covers /api/content at 8 VUs and does not cover the 20 s calibration levels (§5.1) or the 120 s Arm C runs, where a single-run discard on runs that short is the least defensible part of the method. Citing this work would also convert a methodological weakness into a stated, bounded threat rather than an unexamined convention.

sources.citation: A. Maricq, D. Duplyakin, I. Jimenez, C. Maltzahn, R. Stutsman, and R. Ricci, "Taming performance variability," in Proc. 13th USENIX Symp. Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI '18), 2018.
sources.paper_claim: §7 Repeat counts; §7 "Background load and power configuration... adding variance not quantified here"; §4.1 shared-host environment.
sources.what_it_says: An empirical study of roughly 900,000 data points from 835 servers over ten months, characterising the types and magnitudes of performance variability and their effect on confidence in experimental results. The authors provide a statistical model and tooling (CONFIRM) that recommends experiment parameters - in particular how many repetitions a given experiment needs - from the variability actually observed, rather than from a fixed convention.
sources.why_it_matters: This is the systems-side counterpart to Kalibera and Jones and the more directly citable one for a load-testing paper, because it is about server workloads rather than JVM microbenchmarks. It gives the paper a concrete, defensible way to answer a supervisor asking "why four runs?" - run the recommendation procedure over the retained repeats and report the number it returns, or report the achieved CI width and concede where it is too wide. It also sharpens §7's "Background load and power configuration" paragraph, which currently admits unquantified variance and then argues it away with "conditions were identical across arms"; that argument is about differential bias only, and this source shows why the residual common-mode variance still has to be measured before small-n comparisons are trusted. Note it does not vindicate n = 4: the finding is that required trial counts are workload- and machine-specific and frequently larger than researchers assume.

sources.citation: ACM SIGPLAN ad hoc Committee on Programming Language Research Empirical Evaluations (S. M. Blackburn, chair; E. D. Berger, M. Hauswirth, M. W. Hicks), "Empirical evaluation guidelines" and the SIGPLAN Empirical Evaluation Checklist, ACM SIGPLAN, v1.0, Oct. 26, 2018. [Online]. Available: https://www.sigplan.org/Resources/EmpiricalEvaluation/
sources.paper_claim: §4.2 Instrumentation and data handling; §4.3 Statistical treatment; §5 result tables; §7 Threats to Validity; Appendix A Reproducibility.
sources.what_it_says: A community checklist of seven categories for empirical evaluation in systems and languages research: clearly stated claims, suitable comparisons, principled benchmark choice, adequate data analysis, relevant metrics, appropriate experimental design, and appropriate presentation of results. Under "Adequate Data Analysis" the named items include "Sufficient Number of Trials", "Appropriate Summary Statistics" and "Report Data Distribution" - the last on the ground that a central-tendency figure alone does not convey the non-determinism, so variability measures, quantiles or confidence intervals are needed.
sources.why_it_matters: This is the standard reporting checklist to audit the paper against, and the result is mixed rather than bad. "Report Data Distribution" is met unusually well: the paper reports p50/p95/p99/p99.9/p99.99 ladders, per-request series preserved without aggregation or sampling (§4.2), a sampling-unit analysis (§5.9) and a load-model control (§5.8). "Appropriate Presentation" is met - the negative results (H1, H2 refuted) are foregrounded, which is what the checklist asks for. "Sufficient Number of Trials" is the item that fails, and it fails for the same reason across every arm: trial counts were set by time budget (see the study's own decision log, C:\Users\USER\perf-web\docs\decision_log.md D-entries on the scaled arm, which record 24 runs ≈ 50 min as the constraint) and never revisited statistically, even after D21 raised Arm D from n = 2 to n = 5. Citing the checklist and stating item-by-item where the study lands would be a stronger §7 than the current prose, and costs no new measurement.

sources.citation: R. L. Wasserstein and N. A. Lazar, "The ASA statement on p-values: context, process, and purpose," The American Statistician, vol. 70, no. 2, pp. 129-133, 2016. doi: 10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108.
sources.paper_claim: §4.3 "Effect size (rank-biserial r) is reported alongside p, because at the sample sizes involved (millions of requests) statistical significance is uninformative"; §5.4 "The Mann-Whitney test returns p = 0... on an effect size of r = 0.0417, which is negligible. At 4.2 million samples any difference at all attains significance."
sources.what_it_says: The formal position of the American Statistical Association, stating six principles, of which principle 5 is that a p-value or statistical significance does not measure the size of an effect or the importance of a result, and principle 4 that inference should not rest on whether a p-value passes a threshold. It calls for reporting the magnitude and practical relevance of an effect alongside any test.
sources.why_it_matters: The paper's §5.4 argument - p = 0 alongside r = 0.0417, therefore no degradation - is exactly the reasoning this statement endorses, and citing it moves that passage from a plausible-sounding aside to a position backed by the statistics profession rather than only by Georges et al. [9] and Hoefler and Belli [10]. Pairing Mann-Whitney with rank-biserial r is a correct and conventional non-parametric combination, so the choice of test and effect-size measure is sound. Two caveats an examiner may raise, both worth pre-empting: the 4.2 million samples in §5.4 are consecutive requests within one run, so they are autocorrelated and are not independent replicates - the effective sample size is far smaller than n suggests, which is a second and independent reason the p-value there is meaningless, and worth saying in addition to the large-n reason already given. And the ASA's positive recommendation is to report the effect magnitude with its uncertainty; the paper reports r as a bare point value, so it satisfies the letter of "report an effect size" but not the interval that Kalibera and Jones ask for.

sources.citation: Z. M. Jiang and A. E. Hassan, "A survey on load testing of large-scale software systems," IEEE Trans. Softw. Eng., vol. 41, no. 11, pp. 1091-1118, 2015. doi: 10.1109/TSE.2015.2445340.
sources.paper_claim: §2 Gap: "The practitioner literature argues for percentiles largely from first principles and from observational data on production systems, where the cause of any degradation is not controlled."
sources.what_it_says: A survey of research techniques across the three phases of a load test - designing a proper load, executing the load test, and analysing the results - covering how load test results are analysed and compared in the research literature as distinct from practitioner tooling.
sources.why_it_matters: The paper's related-work section (§2) draws on Dean and Barroso, the Google SRE book, Tene, the k6 docs, Schroeder et al., Little, ISO standards and three PL/HPC benchmarking-methodology papers. There is no citation from the software-engineering load-testing literature, which is the field this study actually sits in, and the §2 "Gap" claim is stated against practitioner literature only - an examiner can reasonably ask whether the gap survives contact with the academic load-testing corpus. This survey is the standard entry point to that corpus and is where the load-test-analysis prior art is catalogued. It does not conflict with any finding in the paper - I found nothing that anticipates the uniform-cost versus concentrated-cost decomposition, which remains the paper's distinctive contribution - but citing it, and narrowing the Gap sentence to say what the academic literature has and has not done, would close the most obvious hole in the related-work section. sources.citation: M. Kogias, S. Mallon, and E. Bugnion, "Lancet: A self-correcting latency measuring tool," in Proc. 2019 USENIX Annual Technical Conf. (USENIX ATC '19), Renton, WA, Jul. 2019, pp. 881-896. [Online]. Available: https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc19/presentation/kogias-lancet
sources.paper_claim: Section 5.8: that repeating /api/content with k6's constant-arrival-rate executor at three offered rates constitutes a coordinated-omission-free control that bounds the bias in the closed-model arms; and the 1400/s cell (26,226 dropped iterations, mean 2,276.5 ms) read as a genuine measurement of the server's saturation cliff.
sources.what_it_says: Lancet measures open-loop tail latency for microsecond-scale datacentre applications and is 'self-correcting as it relies on online statistical tests to determine situations in which tail latency cannot be accurately measured' - explicitly including cases where the workload configuration, the client infrastructure, or the application itself makes valid measurement impossible. It determines warm-up length, measurement duration and sampling rate automatically rather than leaving them to the operator, uses NIC hardware timestamping (or a busy-polling latency agent) to remove client-side stack delay, and reports the 99th percentile with a stated confidence interval rather than as a point value.
sources.why_it_matters: Directly relevant to a gap in the paper's control arm. A constant-arrival-rate executor is not automatically coordinated-omission-free: when the generator cannot place iterations, the requests it drops are dropped precisely because the system is slow, which is the same coordination the open model is supposed to remove. The paper reports 26,226 dropped iterations in the 1400/s cell and attributes them to the generator, but never connects that to coordinated omission, and then uses that cell's 501x figure as evidence about the server. Lancet's premise is that a measuring tool must first prove the tail is measurable at all under the given client configuration. Two further points bear on this study: percentiles should carry confidence intervals (the paper reports Arm E p99 as a point value from n=2 while noting it 'varied substantially between the two retained runs'), and client-stack timestamping error matters at the sub-millisecond scale at which Arm C's conclusions are drawn (p99 differences of 1.506 ms vs 1.506 ms, p99.9 of 2.008 vs 2.000 ms). Note: usenix.org blocks automated fetching (HTTP 403); title, all three authors with affiliations, venue, date and abstract were confirmed on the fetched conference programme page above, and independently on the first author's publication list at https://marioskogias.github.io/.

sources.citation: G. Tene, "wrk2: A constant throughput, correct latency recording variant of wrk," GitHub repository. [Online]. Available: https://github.com/giltene/wrk2
sources.paper_claim: Section 2 and Section 5.8: the paper's definition of coordinated omission - 'when a generator's request issuance is coupled to the system's responses, the requests that would have been issued during a slow period are never issued, so slow periods are under-sampled and percentiles are biased optimistically' - and the implicit position that switching to an open-model executor is what corrects it.
sources.what_it_says: The README, by the author of the talk the paper cites as [4], states that conventional generators measure latency from the time a request was actually transmitted, so 'high latency responses result in the load generator coordinating with the server to avoid measurement during high latency periods.' wrk2's correction is not simply to run open-loop: it 'measures response latency from the time the transmission should have occurred according to the constant throughput configured for the run,' combining constant-throughput generation with latency measurement that accounts for the intended schedule, recorded losslessly in HdrHistograms so percentiles out to 99.9999 remain meaningful.
sources.why_it_matters: The paper's characterisation is accurate but only half the mechanism, and the missing half changes what the control arm can claim. Coordinated omission is two errors, not one: the omitted requests (which the paper describes), and the surviving requests whose recorded latency starts at actual rather than intended send time, so each retained sample also under-reports the queueing delay it should have accrued. The canonical correction is a change of timing basis plus back-filling the omitted interval (HdrHistogram's expected-interval recording), which is why wrk2 is a constant-throughput generator rather than merely an open-loop one. Because the paper treats 'open model' as synonymous with 'corrected,' its Arm E measures the difference between two load models, not the size of coordinated omission itself, and Section 6.4's advice to 'state the load model used' should be extended to state the timing basis. This is grey literature rather than peer-reviewed, but it is the reference implementation behind reference [4] and is the appropriate citation for the correction the paper does not describe.

sources.citation: J. Leverich and C. Kozyrakis, "Reconciling high server utilization and sub-millisecond quality-of-service," in Proc. 9th European Conf. Computer Systems (EuroSys '14), Amsterdam, The Netherlands, Apr. 2014, art. 4, pp. 1-14. doi: 10.1145/2592798.2592821.
sources.paper_claim: Section 4.4 and Section 7: that a load generator sharing a host with the system under test can be mistaken for server saturation, and that the Node process's CPU plateau is sufficient evidence that the queue forms in the application rather than in k6.
sources.what_it_says: Section 3.1 describes the mutilate load generator, in which 'requests are paced using an exponential distribution' rather than issued back-to-back, and states the design constraint explicitly: the generator is configured with hundreds to thousands of connections across 20 client machines so that it can 'saturate it and observe server-side queuing delay, while never taxing the clients enough to see client-side queuing delay.' The paper's latency breakdown (Table 1) decomposes an average request into driver RX, TCP/IP, epoll wait, libevent queuing, read, execution and write time, showing that under load 'the vast majority of the latency when memcached is overloaded is queuing delay' located in libevent and epoll.
sources.why_it_matters: This is the standard rigorous precedent for the control the paper attempts in Section 4.4, and it sets a higher bar in two ways. First, it separates client-side from server-side queueing by construction - dedicated client machines and headroom - rather than inferring it after the fact from a CPU plateau; the paper's generator and server share one desktop, and a plateau at 1.4 cores shows Node is not gaining CPU but does not by itself exclude k6-induced scheduling delay on the same host. Second, it attributes latency to a specific queue by instrumenting the server's own path, which is the technique that would let the paper distinguish the self-queueing effect it flags as an unresolved caveat in Arm C. Worth flagging for the student: Treadmill (ISCA '16, Table I) classifies mutilate as a closed-loop controller despite its exponential pacing, so this source should be cited for client/server queueing separation, not as evidence that pacing arrivals makes a generator open-loop - a distinction the paper currently collapses.

sources.citation: M. Fruth, S. Scherzinger, W. Mauerer, and R. Ramsauer, "Tell-tale tail latencies: Pitfalls and perils in database benchmarking," in Performance Evaluation and Benchmarking (TPCTC 2021), Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol. 13169, Cham: Springer, 2022, pp. 119-134. doi: 10.1007/978-3-030-94437-7_8. Preprint: arXiv:2107.11607.
sources.paper_claim: Section 5.6 (a slow path below ~1% incidence is invisible to p99) and Section 7 (background load and power configuration on a shared desktop host add 'variance not quantified here').
sources.what_it_says: Measuring YCSB and TPC-C against MariaDB and PostgreSQL through the Java-based OLTPBench harness (itself run 'in a closed-loop fashion'), the authors find that the choice of JVM and garbage collector in the harness alone shifts maximum latencies by up to several orders of magnitude 'while the usually considered quantities median, 95th and 99th percentile of the observed latency distribution remain largely unperturbed.' They trace almost every latency above 10 ms to harness GC pauses by matching OLTPBench's series against the JVM log, and argue for time-resolved rather than summary measurement so that events can be attributed to the component that caused them.
sources.why_it_matters: Two direct bearings. First, it is independent empirical support for the paper's sharpest and most defensible result - that rare high-cost events sit below p99 and are invisible to it - arrived at from the opposite direction: there the invisible sub-1% events were injected by the measuring instrument and went unnoticed precisely because p50/p95/p99 stayed flat. Second, it raises the bar on the paper's threats-to-validity section. Node has a garbage collector too, the paper's Arm C tails are in the 2-20 ms range on a shared desktop under an unquantified background load, and the paper's own soak arm reports GC keeping pace with per-quarter memory means. Fruth et al. show that at this scale the runtime and the harness can own the extreme tail outright, so the paper's Arm C p99.99 and 'percent over 3 ms' figures cannot be attributed to the application without an instrument-noise floor - which the study could establish cheaply, since its 100%-cheap /robots.txt workload is close to the NoOp control Fruth et al. use for exactly this purpose. It also supports Section 5.9's argument for stating the sampling unit, from a time-resolved-measurement angle.

With p = 0.99 and q = 0.001 it is exactly "a 0.1% slow path is invisible to p99." It establishes that the claim is a definitional/theorem-level property of quantiles rather than an empirical finding, so the paper cannot present it as a result. The paper should cite it as a known constraint and reframe its own contribution as an empirical demonstration of the boundary on a real system.

sources.citation: E. D. Berger, S. M. Blackburn, M. Hauswirth, and M. Available: https://www.sigplan.org/Resources/EmpiricalEvaluation/
sources.paper_claim: §4.5 experimental arms and executor choice; §5.8 Arm E open-model control; §7 Threats to Validity ("Closed-model measurement", "Repeat counts"); §5 result tables; §6.4 Implications for practice.
sources.why_it_matters: This is the reporting standard to audit the paper against, and the audit is mostly favourable - which makes the two failures cheap to fix and worth stating. The strongest and most specific hit is one the proposing agent missed entirely: the checklist's "Gated workload generator" item independently endorses the paper's §5.8 argument from the reviewing side, so Arm E is not merely a nice control but a stated community requirement that most of the paper's own arms do not meet, and §7's "Closed-model measurement" paragraph should say so. "No data distribution reported" is met unusually well (p50/p95/p99/p99.9/p99.99 ladders, per-request series preserved without aggregation or sampling per §4.2, the §5.9 sampling-unit analysis) but is violated at the level of across-run spread, and "Insufficient number of trials" is the item that plainly fails, for the same reason across every arm: trial counts were set by time budget and never revisited statistically. The study's own decision log records this explicitly - docs/decision_log.md D-entry at line 128 ("24 runs ~ 50 min") sets the scaled arm to 2 kept repeats for cost reasons, and D21 later raised n to 5 at ×1/×10/×100 by merging extra runs, still without a statistical basis. An item-by-item §7 against this checklist would be stronger than the current prose and costs no new measurement. Two corrections to the proposing agent's version: the checklist names its entries as violations ("Insufficient number of trials", "Inappropriate summary statistics", "No data distribution reported"), not as the positive forms quoted; and the checklist PDF's credit line reads Berger, Blackburn, Hauswirth and Hicks, October 2018, so "Blackburn, chair" belongs to the Guidelines document rather than the checklist.
sources.what_it_says: A seven-category community checklist for empirical evaluation in programming-languages and systems research, with example violations in each category. Under "Adequate Data Analysis" the violations are "Insufficient number of trials" (non-deterministic systems may need many trials; failure risks treating noise as signal, and trials may be needed to get the system into its intended state to avoid warm-up effects), "Inappropriate summary statistics", and "No data distribution reported" (a measure of variability, quantiles or confidence intervals is needed, because a central-tendency figure alone can mislead when the distribution is bimodal or has significant variance). Under "Appropriate and Clear Experimental Design" it lists "Gated workload generator": load generators for transaction-oriented systems should be open-loop and issue work independently of the system under test, or results are likely to mislead.
