sources.paper_claim: §3 System Under Test, l.167-171: 'Every such request performs a file read and a synchronous `JSON.parse`, and `JSON.parse` blocks Node's single-threaded event loop. Per-request cost therefore becomes queueing under concurrency, while dataset size becomes per-request cost.' Also §5.5, l.395-397: 'That is `JSON.parse` behaving as an O(n) operation, and the mean reports it faithfully.'
sources.what_it_says: Official Node.js documentation, published by the OpenJS Foundation and Node.js contributors. States: '`JSON.parse` and `JSON.stringify` are other potentially expensive operations. While these are `O(n)` in the length of the input, for large `n` they can take surprisingly long', and 'If your server manipulates JSON objects, particularly those from a client, you should be cautious about the size of the objects or strings you work with on the Event Loop.' It gives a measured example on a 50 MB stringified object — 0.7 s to stringify, 0.03 s to indexOf, 1.3 s to parse. On the queueing consequence: 'Because Node.js handles many clients with few threads, if a thread blocks handling one client's request, then pending client requests may not get a turn until the thread finishes its callback or task', and 'While a thread is blocked working on behalf of one client, it cannot handle requests from any other clients.'
sources.why_it_matters: This is the primary-source citation the paper's central mechanism currently lacks entirely — §3 asserts both the event-loop blocking and the O(n) parse cost with no reference at all, and every arm in the study depends on that mechanism being real. The 'it cannot handle requests from any other clients' sentence is the documented basis for the queueing that produces the uniform-slowdown regime the paper reports in §5.1 and §5.5, and the explicit O(n) statement backs the near-linear mean across three orders of dataset scale in §5.5 (Table, ×1 to ×1000). Caveat: pair this with the Davis et al. citation below only knowingly — the two share authorship lineage (see that entry), so they are not two independent confirmations.

findings.title: "Tail divergence" names two different ratios, and §6.2 puts numbers from both side by side
findings.location: §5.1 table caption "Tail divergence (p99/p50) across the calibration sweep"; §5.5 "Tail divergence, meanwhile, collapses from 2.55 to 1.13"; §6.2 "Tail divergence peaked at 4 virtual users (3.85) and fell to 1.17 at 200. The same inversion appears across dataset scale."
findings.problem: The term is never defined, and it is used for p99/p50 in the calibration sweep but for p99/mean in Arm D and the abstract. §6.2 then quotes 3.85 and 1.17 (p99/p50) in one sentence and asserts "the same inversion" for dataset scale, whose numbers (2.55 to 1.13) are p99/mean. A reader comparing 3.85 against 2.55 as the same quantity is being misled by the paper's own vocabulary, and §6.4 compounds it by recommending "a ratio of percentiles, p99/p50" as if that were the ratio the results section reported throughout.
findings.evidence: §5.1's table is captioned "(p99/p50)" and its row reads 1.95 / 2.18 / 3.85 / 3.47 / 2.32 / 1.17. The 2.55 and 1.13 in §5.5 come from the "p99/mean" column of the Arm D table (×1: mean 6.47, p99 16.51 = 2.55; ×100: 528.75 / 597.01 = 1.13), and the abstract states the same pair as "The ratio of p99 to mean falls from 2.55 to 1.13". Arm A's table also carries a "p99/mean" column (1.72 to 4.63), so three different tables label divergence two different ways.
findings.fix: Define the term once in §4.3 (e.g. "tail divergence = p99/p50 unless stated") and tag every use: "tail divergence (p99/p50)" in §5.1/§6.2, "tail-to-mean ratio (p99/mean)" in §5.2/§5.5/abstract/conclusion. In §6.2, replace "The same inversion appears across dataset scale" with the explicit p99/mean figures so the reader is not invited to compare 3.85 with 2.55.

findings.title: "Invisible to a percentile below its own incidence" states the opposite of the rule derived two lines later, and the same wording carries the Fig. 7 caption
findings.location: §5.6 "A slow path is invisible to a percentile below its own incidence (Fig. 7)"; Fig. 7 caption "Arm C. A slow path is invisible to any percentile below its own incidence."
findings.problem: Read literally, "a percentile below its own incidence" means rank p < incidence q — for a 0.1% slow path that would be percentiles below p0.1, which is not what happens. The rule the paper actually derives is about rank relative to 100 − incidence. The sentence and the figure caption therefore say something false in isolation, and the caption is the one piece of text a reader skimming the figures will take away.
findings.evidence: The very next sentence gives the correct boundary: "A percentile at rank *p* can only reflect a slow path affecting a fraction *q* of requests if *p* > 100(1 − *q*)." The Arm C data follow that form, not the loose one: at 10% incidence the p90 column reads 2.580 ms against 1.003 ms for 100% cheap (visible at rank 90 = 100 − 10), and at 0.1% incidence p99 reads 1.506 ms, identical to the pure-cheap workload's 1.506 ms, because 99 < 100 − 0.1.
findings.fix: Change both the body sentence and the Fig. 7 caption to the rank form, e.g. "A slow path affecting a fraction q of requests is invisible to any percentile at a rank below 100(1 − q): a 0.1% slow path leaves p99 unchanged." The caption should also name the arm's workloads so it stands alone.

findings.title: The abstract and the §4.5 table caption say "six" arms; the table lists eight rows and the Fig. 2 caption implies eight
findings.location: Abstract "under six controlled load arms and 39.4 million requests"; §4.5 caption "The six experimental arms and the variable each isolates."; Fig. 2 caption "Five arms vary uniform cost; only Arm C varies its distribution."
findings.problem: A caption that miscounts the rows of the table it sits on cannot stand alone, and the reader who counts is left unsure whether two arms were dropped from the paper or two extra ones added. The two captions are also mutually inconsistent.
findings.evidence: The §4.5 table has eight rows: Calibration, A load matrix, Stress, Soak, D dataset scale, C variance injection, B rate limiting, E open-loop control. §5 reports all eight (§5.1 calibration through §5.8 Arm E). Fig. 2's "Five arms vary uniform cost" only adds up if Calibration, A, Stress, Soak and D are all counted as arms — which gives eight in total, not six. FINDINGS.md line 19 carries the same "Six controlled arms" wording, so the error is inherited rather than introduced, but its own section headings list Calibration, Arm A, Soak, Stress, Arm D, Arm C, Arm B, Arm E — eight.
findings.fix: Either say "eight" in both places, or, if the intent is that calibration and stress are not hypothesis-testing arms, state that explicitly: "Six experimental arms, plus a calibration sweep and a stress run." Make the abstract, the table caption and Fig. 2's caption use the same count.

findings.title: Three direct quotations and attributions in §1 carry no reference numbers, though the same sources are numbered in §2
findings.location: §1 "Google's *Site Reliability Engineering* states plainly that ... 'it's entirely possible for most of the requests to be fast, but for a long tail of requests to be much, much slower' ... '5% of requests are 20 times slower'"; "Dean and Barroso's account of tail latency in large-scale services"; "ISO/IEC 25010 defines performance efficiency as ..."
findings.problem: Quoted material is presented without a citation marker at first use. The citation style elsewhere in the paper is numeric-at-first-mention, so the introduction reads as inconsistent with the rest of the document and the quotations are formally unsourced at the point they are made.
findings.evidence: §1 contains exactly one bracketed citation, [1], on ISO/IEC 25023. The same three sources are numbered in §2: "Dean and Barroso [2]", "Google's SRE practice [3]", "ISO/IEC 25010 [8]". §2 quotes SRE with the marker attached ("Google's SRE practice [3] recommends ... noting that 'a high-order percentile ...'"), which is the pattern §1 breaks.
findings.fix: Add [3] to both SRE quotations, [2] to the Dean and Barroso sentence, and [8] to the ISO/IEC 25010 sentence in §1. If IEEE first-citation ordering is being kept, renumber so the introduction's citations come first.

findings.title: The ISO/IEC 25010 definition and the 25023 sentence are reproduced almost verbatim in §1 and again in §2
findings.location: §1 "performs its functions within specified time and throughput parameters and is efficient in the use of resources" / "The companion measurement standard ISO/IEC 25023 [1] defines mean response time as a quality measure against that sub-characteristic."; §2 "Standards context" paragraph
findings.problem: The same quotation, the same *time behaviour* attribution and the same 25023 sentence appear twice within ninety lines, so §2's "Standards context" paragraph adds no information beyond the closing question. The abstract states it a third time.
findings.evidence: §1: 'ISO/IEC 25010 defines performance efficiency as the degree to which a product "performs its functions within specified time and throughput parameters and is efficient in the use of resources" under specified conditions, and places response time under its *time behaviour* sub-characteristic. The companion measurement standard ISO/IEC 25023 [1] defines mean response time as a quality measure against that sub-characteristic.' §2: 'ISO/IEC 25010 [8] defines performance efficiency as the degree to which a product "performs its functions within specified time and throughput parameters and is efficient in the use of resources" under specified conditions. Its *time behaviour* sub-characteristic covers ... ISO/IEC 25023 [1] defines mean response time as a measure against that sub-characteristic.' The quoted clause is word-for-word identical; the template (paper_template.md) shows no placeholder difference between them.
findings.fix: Keep the full definition and both citations in §2's "Standards context" paragraph, and cut §1 to a single sentence that cites forward — e.g. "Response time is a standardised quality measure: ISO/IEC 25010 [8] places it under *time behaviour* and ISO/IEC 25023 [1] defines mean response time against it (§2)." Retain only the last sentence of §2's paragraph, which states the paper's question.

findings.title: Contribution 3 — the "sharpest result" (latency needs an error-rate denominator) is textbook Google SRE, from the same book the paper already cites
findings.location: §1.2 Contribution 3, "establishing that no latency statistic is interpretable without an error-rate denominator"; §8, "The sharpest result concerns neither statistic"; §6.3 heading "No latency statistic survives without an error rate"
findings.problem: The paper presents as its strongest, most novel result the claim that latency statistics are meaningless without an error rate, and that a fast rejection makes a dashboard look better while the service fails. This is stated verbatim, with the identical fast-error mechanism, in the Four Golden Signals section of Site Reliability Engineering — the book the paper cites as [3]. The paper cites only Chapter 4 ("Service Level Objectives") of that book and never cites Chapter 6 ("Monitoring Distributed Systems"), which contains the exact result. A reviewer who knows the SRE book will read this as the author not having read past the chapter that supported his framing.
findings.evidence: I fetched https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/ . It states: "It's important to distinguish between the latency of successful requests and the latency of failed requests", and gives the mechanism the paper rediscovers in §5.7: "an HTTP 500 error triggered due to loss of connection to a database or other critical backend might be served very quickly; however, as an HTTP 500 error indicates a failed request, factoring 500s into your overall latency might result in misleading calculations", concluding "a slow error is even worse than a fast error!" The paper's §5.7 mechanism — "A rejection really is cheaper to produce than a search: it is written from a fixed string and returns before the handler reads content.json" — is the same phenomenon with 429 substituted for 500. Reference [3] in the paper is scoped to "ch. 4, 'Service Level Objectives'" (paper.md line 748-750), so the golden-signals chapter is absent from the bibliography.
findings.fix: Demote this from a contribution to a quantified confirmation. Cite the SRE book's Four Golden Signals chapter explicitly in §2 and in §6.3, state that the principle is established practice, and claim only what is actually new: the magnitude (52.8x mean improvement, 21.3x p99 improvement at 99.998% failure, from facts.json armb values) and the specific demonstration that percentiles fail here in the *same direction* as the mean rather than correcting it. Rewrite Contribution 3 as "a quantified worked example of a known monitoring hazard", and remove "establishing that" and "The sharpest result".

findings.title: Contribution 2 — "tail divergence decreases under heavy load" is a known property of closed-model load generation, established by the paper's own reference [6], and is measured only under that model
findings.location: §1.2 Contribution 2, "That reverses the intuition that percentiles matter most when a system is most stressed"; §6.2 "This is counter-intuitive, and mechanically obvious in hindsight"
findings.problem: Presented as a counter-intuitive empirical discovery. It is (a) already published for closed-model workloads by Schroeder, Wierman and Harchol-Balter, which the paper cites as [6] but summarises only as "open and closed workload models produce substantially different behaviour", omitting that the specific difference is tail suppression in the closed model; and (b) measured entirely under a closed-model executor, so the trend may be an artefact of the harness rather than a property of the system. §7's blanket defence ("The bias direction is optimistic, meaning reported tail divergences are conservative") does not rescue the *trend*: if closed-model tail compression worsens as concurrency rises, the declining p99/p50 curve is partly manufactured by the instrument, and Arm E measured only one point (8 VUs vs 1100/s), which cannot establish that the bias factor is constant across 1 to 200 VUs.
findings.evidence: Schroeder et al. (NSDI '06, the paper's [6]) report that for a given load the tail is much longer in the open case than the closed one, and that a very high multiprogramming level is needed before a closed system approaches open-system response times — i.e. bounded concurrency suppresses the tail by construction (https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/nsdi06/tech/schroeder.html). The paper's own numbers show the same instrument effect: facts.json arma_api_content_v8_p99 = 15.097 ms (closed, 8 VUs, 1,174 req/s) against arme_1100_p99 = 36.685 ms (open, 1,099 req/s) — the paper itself calls this "a factor of 2.43" in §5.8. The paper also supplies the mechanical explanation in its own text: §5.1 "latency rises in proportion to concurrency… That is Little's Law with throughput pinned", which forces W ≈ N/X for every request and so drives p99/p50 toward 1 by arithmetic, not by discovery. Divergence values checked in facts.json: calib_ratio_4 = 3.85 falling to calib_ratio_200 = 1.17.
findings.fix: In §2, expand the [6] summary to say that closed models specifically suppress tail latency relative to open models. In §5.1 and §6.2, restate the finding as conditional: "under closed-model load with bounded concurrency, tail divergence peaks near the knee and falls" — and state plainly that the study cannot show the same holds open-loop, because Arm E sampled a single operating point. Either add open-loop divergence measurements at two or three concurrency-equivalent rates, or drop the word "reverses the intuition" and re-scope Contribution 2 to a replication of a known closed-model property on a real application.

findings.title: Contribution 1 — "the mean conceals variance, not slowness" is the framing of both cited sources, and the paper concedes it in §2
findings.location: §1.2 Contribution 1, "showing that the mean fails only for the latter"; §1.1 "The refutations are the substantive contribution"; §6.1 blockquote "It fails specifically, and severely, when a minority of requests carry disproportionate cost"
findings.problem: The central refined claim is presented as the study's substantive contribution, but the paper itself states in §2 that this is already Dean and Barroso's position, and the SRE quote it reproduces locates the problem in variance too. At root the claim is also definitional: the mean is a location statistic, so it tracks a uniform location shift exactly, and a mixture's mean is by construction the weight-averaged mean of its components. A reviewer will see the contribution restated in the related-work section as prior art two pages earlier.
findings.evidence: paper.md §2, lines 103-107: "Dean and Barroso [2] … Their concern is variability, not mean slowness, a distinction this paper takes as its central axis." And §2 lines 112-114 quoting [3]: "people typically prefer a slightly slower system to one with high variance in response time", followed by the paper's own words "again locating the problem in variance". I confirmed the SRE Chapter 4 text at https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/ ("A simple average can obscure these tail latencies"). The standard statistical treatment of exactly this — a mean falling between two modes and describing neither — is elementary textbook material on bimodal/mixture distributions (e.g. https://statisticsbyjim.com/basics/bimodal-distribution/).
findings.fix: Reframe Contribution 1 around what is genuinely new: not the qualitative claim, but the controlled single-system decomposition that holds total work constant and varies only its distribution (Arm C), and the quantified dilution asymmetry — mean falls 6.51x while p99.9 falls 1.47x for identical work, a 4.4x optimism gap. Say explicitly in §1.2 that the qualitative distinction is due to [2] and [3] and that this study supplies the controlled measurement they lack. Delete "showing that the mean fails only for the latter" as a discovery claim and delete "The refutations are the substantive contribution" from §1.1, or restrict it to H1 and H2, which are genuinely the study's own hypotheses.

findings.title: The "p99 is blind to a 0.1% slow path" result is definitional, and the paper proves it analytically before measuring it
findings.location: Abstract, "A further result constrains the recommended remedy. A slow path affecting 0.1% of requests was entirely invisible to p99"; §5.6 "The data follow that boundary exactly"
findings.problem: This is stated in the abstract and conclusion as an empirical result, but it is a tautology of what a quantile is, and the paper says so itself: it derives the rule p > 100(1 − q) from first principles and then reports that the data obey it. Confirming a definition is not a result. It is also standard practitioner knowledge that a one-in-a-thousand event requires p99.9 rather than p99. Presenting it as a discovery in the abstract invites a reviewer to distrust the other claims.
findings.evidence: paper.md §5.6, lines 432-436: "A percentile at rank p can only reflect a slow path affecting a fraction q of requests if p > 100(1 − q). The data follow that boundary exactly" — the analytic statement precedes the measurement, so the measurement can only confirm arithmetic. Web check confirms this is common practitioner knowledge: P99 "by design cannot detect problems affecting less than 1% of requests", and 0.1% events "appear around the P99.9 mark" (https://aerospike.com/blog/what-is-p99-latency/ , https://blog.openresty.com/en/p99-latency/). The measured numbers do sit exactly on the boundary as expected — facts.json Arm C: 99.9/0.1 mix p99 = 1.506 ms, 100% cheap p99 = 1.506 ms, identical to three decimals.
findings.fix: Move the boundary rule to §4.3 as a stated analytic property of percentiles, and present §5.6's numbers as an empirical validation that the instrument and the workload behave as the definition requires — which is a legitimate sanity check, not a finding. In the abstract and §8, replace "A further result" with wording that credits the definition, e.g. "as follows from the definition of a quantile and is confirmed here". Keep the genuinely non-obvious part of §5.6 — the self-queueing caveat at lines 452-458, where rare expensive requests are individually faster — and give that the emphasis the tautology currently gets.

findings.title: Contribution 4's "percentile sampling bias" is Tene's mechanism restated, and the reported bias magnitude is an artefact of bucket averaging
findings.location: §1.2 Contribution 4, "a measurement of percentile sampling bias arising from time-varying request rates"; §5.9 "A percentile is therefore not one well-defined quantity"
findings.problem: Two problems. First, the mechanism claimed as a separate contribution is the one the paper attributes to Tene [4] in §2 — fast periods over-sampled, slow periods under-sampled, percentiles biased optimistically — so Contribution 4 double-counts one piece of prior art as two. Second, the quantity actually measured is not sampling bias. Per-second means over roughly a thousand requests each are, by the central limit theorem, concentrated tightly around the overall mean, so their p99 must land near the mean regardless of the tail; the reported "bias" measures how much averaging destroys, not how the sampling unit shifts the percentile. The soak run had zero errors and no degradation (degradation ratio 0.9944), so there were no slow periods to under-sample — the mechanism §5.9 invokes cannot be what produced the number.
findings.evidence: paper.md §2, lines 116-120 attributes to Tene: "slow periods are under-sampled and percentiles are biased optimistically"; §5.9 line 547 restates it: "Percentiles computed over raw request samples over-represent fast periods, because more requests complete per unit time when the system is healthy." The arithmetic: facts.json soak_rps = 1172 and soak_span_s = 3599, so each one-second bucket averages ~1,172 samples; soak_p99_quant = 7.26 ms sits essentially at soak_mean = 6.814 ms, not at soak_p99 = 17.436 ms. The smoke run repeats the pattern — smoke_requests 30,317 over 30 s (~1,010 per bucket), smoke_p99_quant = 1.041 vs smoke_mean = 0.959. In both cases the time-quantized p99 is pinned to the mean by bucket size, which is what the CLT predicts and what the paper's own claim of "bias" does not distinguish from.
findings.fix: Split Contribution 4: keep the coordinated-omission measurement (Arm E) as the contribution, and drop the sampling-bias half or demote it to a methodological note. In §5.9, either re-derive the comparison with a bucket size small enough that the per-bucket sampling distribution does not collapse to the mean (or use per-second p99 rather than per-second mean as the quantized unit), or state explicitly that the gap reported is dominated by within-bucket averaging and therefore bounds nothing about sampling unit choice. The recommendation at §6.4 item 3 ("State the sampling unit for percentiles") is sound and can stand on the definitional argument alone, without the unsupported magnitude.

findings.title: Direct quotations in the Introduction carry no citation markers (breaches brief requirements 8 and 10)
findings.location: §1 Introduction, paper.md lines 48-60: "performs its functions within specified time and throughput parameters and is efficient in the use of resources"; "it's entirely possible for most of the requests to be fast, but for a long tail of requests to be much, much slower"; "5% of requests are 20 times slower"
findings.problem: Three verbatim quotations appear in the Introduction with quotation marks but no reference number. The ISO/IEC 25010 wording is quoted with no [8]; two direct quotes from the SRE book are attributed only as "Google's Site Reliability Engineering states plainly that..." with no [3]; Dean and Barroso are named in the next sentence with no [2]. The brief's requirement 8 is "All sources must be properly cited" and requirement 10 is "Properly acknowledge and cite all external sources". Quoted text without a citation at the point of use is the single easiest thing for a marker (or a similarity checker) to flag, and it reads as an originality problem rather than a formatting slip.
findings.evidence: Checked paper.md lines 48-52 and 55-60: the only bracketed marker in that whole passage is "[1]" attached to ISO/IEC 25023. §2 (line 134) quotes the identical ISO 25010 sentence and there it does carry "[8]", and §2 line 109 cites SRE as "[3]" — so the references exist and are correct, they are simply missing in §1. I confirmed this is not a build artefact: paper_template.md lines 47-60 have the same gap, and diffing paper_template.pre_refs.md against paper_template.md over lines 44-62 shows the late reference-adding pass rewrote exactly this paragraph to insert "[1]" and left the surrounding quotations unmarked.
findings.fix: In paper_template.md §1, attach markers at the point of quotation: "...efficient in the use of resources" [8]; "...much, much slower" [3]; "5% of requests are 20 times slower" [3]; "Dean and Barroso's account [2]". No new references are needed — [2], [3] and [8] are already in the list and already used in §2. Then rebuild via build_paper.py and make_docx.py.

findings.title: The paper says "six controlled load arms" but its own arms table and design figure show eight
findings.location: Abstract, paper.md lines 11-12: "using a single real Node.js web application under six controlled load arms"; §4.5 table caption, line 244: "The six experimental arms and the variable each isolates."
findings.problem: The count is wrong and it is wrong in the first paragraph of the abstract, in the §4.5 table caption, and inside Fig. 2 itself. The §4.5 table lists eight rows: Calibration, A (load matrix), Stress, Soak, D (dataset scale), C (variance injection), B (rate limiting), E (open-loop control). No reading of the table yields six — it is eight rows, seven if calibration is excluded as setup, five if only the lettered arms A-E are counted. A marker reads the abstract, counts the table, and the paper has contradicted itself before Section 5.
findings.evidence: Counted the rows of the §4.5 table directly in paper.md lines 246-254: eight data rows. Opened results/figures/fig_experimental_design.png — its header box reads "One application, one host / six controlled arms" above eight labelled boxes (Calibration, Arm A, Stress, Soak, Arm D, Arm C, Arm B, Arm E). The same "Six controlled arms" phrasing propagates from FINDINGS.md ("Six controlled arms, each varying one thing"), so the error is in the source framing, not in substitution — facts.json has no arm-count fact at all.
findings.fix: Pick one definition and apply it everywhere. Simplest correct version: say "eight controlled arms" (or "five experimental arms plus calibration, stress and soak runs") in the abstract line 11, the §4.5 caption line 244, the FINDINGS.md method line, and regenerate fig_experimental_design.png from scripts/make_diagrams.py with the header text corrected.

findings.title: The headline trend is drawn entirely from closed-model data, and the coordinated-omission control bounds the bias at only one operating point
findings.location: §5.8, line 526: "The closed-model percentiles used throughout this paper are therefore optimistic by roughly that factor"; §7, lines 665-667: "The bias direction is optimistic, meaning reported tail divergences are conservative."
findings.problem: The paper's central refuted-hypothesis result is that tail divergence FALLS as load rises (§5.1, §5.5, §6.2). Every measurement supporting that trend is closed-model, and the paper concedes closed-model percentiles are optimistically biased. The coordinated-omission control measures that bias at a single offered rate (1100/s) and then generalises the direction to all arms. But a bias whose magnitude grows with load would compress high-concurrency tails more than low-concurrency ones, which is exactly the shape of the reported trend — so the control as run cannot rule out that the headline finding is partly a load-dependent instrument artefact. The Threats section asserts conservativeness as settled rather than naming this as the open question.
findings.evidence: Arm E in facts.json has three offered rates, not one: arme_600 (mean 1.104, p99 10.274), arme_1100 (mean 4.544, p99 36.685), arme_1400 (mean 2276.513, p99 2735.002). Only the 1100/s cell is compared against closed-model data in §5.8 (against arma_api_content_v8_p99 = 15.097, factor 2.43). The cross-load check is already sitting in the paper's own table and is never computed: p99/mean in the open model falls 9.31 → 8.07 → 1.20 across the three rates, which reproduces the same downward trend the closed-model sweep shows (p99/p50 3.85 at 4 VUs → 1.17 at 200 VUs, facts.json calib_ratio_4 / calib_ratio_200). That is the strongest available defence of the main claim and the paper omits it.
findings.fix: Add two or three sentences to §5.8 computing p99/mean across the three open-model rates (9.31, 8.07, 1.20) and stating that the open model independently reproduces the falling-divergence trend, so the result is not an artefact of the closed executor. Then soften §7 from "the bias direction is optimistic, meaning reported tail divergences are conservative" to a claim that the bias was measured at one operating point, that its load-dependence was not characterised, and that the open-model rates provide a consistency check rather than a correction.

findings.title: §6.1 attributes a falling p99/mean ratio to three sections; only one of them reports that ratio, and the soak reports no trend at all
findings.location: §6.1, lines 607-611: "Where cost rises uniformly, whether through deeper queues (§5.1), larger datasets (§5.5) or sustained load (§5.4), the mean tracks the change faithfully and the ratio of p99 to mean falls."
findings.problem: Of the three sections cited, only §5.5 (Arm D) actually reports p99/mean falling. §5.1 reports p99/p50, a different statistic, in a table explicitly captioned "Tail divergence (p99/p50) across the calibration sweep". §5.4 (soak) is a single steady-state operating point with one ratio and no comparison — nothing falls there, and the section's whole point is that no change occurred. The discussion is therefore claiming support from an arm that measured a different quantity and from an arm that measured no trend.
findings.evidence: Compared the three sections. §5.1 table (paper.md line 283) is labelled p99/p50 with values 1.95/2.18/3.85/3.47/2.32/1.17 (facts.json calib_ratio_*). §5.5 table (line 388) has a p99/mean column falling 2.55 → 1.35 → 1.13 → 1.13 (facts.json scaled_*_ratio). §5.4's soak table (lines 358-366) reports a single mean 6.814 and single p99 17.436 (facts.json soak_mean, soak_p99) with a degradation ratio of 0.9944 — one operating point, no ratio trend of any kind.
findings.fix: Split the sentence: cite §5.1 for p99/p50 falling from 3.85 to 1.17 under deeper queues, cite §5.5 for p99/mean falling from 2.55 to 1.13 across dataset scale, and cite §5.4 separately for what it actually shows — that uniform per-request cost does not accumulate over time, so no divergence develops at all.

findings.title: Calibration plateau throughput is quoted as the 200-VU peak rather than the plateau, contradicting the study's own calibration record
findings.location: §5.1, lines 272-274: "Beyond that point the server delivers approximately 2,116 requests per second regardless of client count"
findings.problem: 2,116 req/s is the single highest value in the sweep, observed only at 200 VUs. At the two concurrency levels the rest of the paper actually uses — 8 and 16 VUs — measured throughput is 1,951 and 1,917 req/s, 8 to 9 per cent below the quoted figure and, at 16 VUs, lower than at 8. Presenting the maximum as the level delivered "regardless of client count" overstates the plateau in the one place the paper establishes the saturation ceiling that Little's Law arguments in §5.3 later rest on.
findings.evidence: docs/calibration.md line 47 states it correctly: "Past 8 VUs the server delivers ~1,950-2,100 req/s no matter how many clients wait." Its results table gives 1,951 (8 VUs), 1,917 (16), 1,946 (32), 2,020 (64), 2,076 (100), 2,075 (150), 2,116 (200). FINDINGS.md also labels it correctly as "Peak throughput 2,116 req/s". facts.json stores the value under the key calib_peak_rps — i.e. the fact file itself calls it a peak, and the paper's prose promoted it to a plateau.
findings.fix: In paper_template.md §5.1, replace "approximately 2,116 requests per second regardless of client count" with the range from calibration.md, e.g. "approximately 1,950 to 2,100 requests per second regardless of client count, peaking at 2,116 at 200 virtual users". If a substituted number is wanted, add a calib_plateau_low / calib_plateau_high pair to collect_facts.py rather than reusing calib_peak_rps.

findings.title: Coordinated-omission correction generalised to the whole paper from two runs that disagree with each other
findings.location: §5.8, "The closed-model percentiles used throughout this paper are therefore optimistic by roughly that factor: coordinated omission is present and measurable. The direction matters for interpretation: every tail divergence reported above is a conservative estimate, and the true divergences are larger, not smaller." Repeated without caveat in §7: "The bias direction is optimistic, meaning reported tail divergences are conservative."
findings.problem: A single-cell, n = 2 comparison on one route (/api/content) at one offered rate is used to assert a directional correction for every percentile in every other arm (calibration, Arm A, soak, Arm D, Arm C, Arm B). The 2.43x factor is the mean of two runs that bracket the closed-model value, so the data do not establish the direction consistently, let alone the magnitude, and the paper's own "Spread caution" three paragraphs later contradicts the sentence quoted.
findings.evidence: C:\Users\USER\perf-web\results\open\index.csv: the two retained (is_warmup=false) 1100/s rows give p99_ms = 56.9385 and 16.4309, whose mean is the 36.685 cited (arme_1100_p99 in paper/facts.json, provenance results/open/index.csv). The closed comparator is 15.097 ms (arma_api_content_v8_p99). So run 3 is 1.09x the closed value (no detectable bias) and run 2 is 3.77x; "a factor of 2.43" averages a 1.09 and a 3.77. §7 further states "The effects reported are large relative to the observed spread", which is false here: the between-run spread (16.4 to 56.9 ms) exceeds the effect claimed.
findings.fix: Restrict the claim to the cell measured. Replace with: "In the one cell where open and closed models were matched (/api/content, ~1100 req/s), the two retained open-model runs gave p99 of 16.4 and 56.9 ms against 15.1 ms closed; the direction is consistent with coordinated omission in one run and indistinguishable in the other, and with n = 2 no correction factor can be carried to the other arms." Delete "every tail divergence reported above is a conservative estimate, and the true divergences are larger, not smaller" and the matching §7 sentence, or restate both as an untested possibility.

findings.title: CV ordering, and the practice recommendation built on it, rests on one run per workload where the deciding gap is inside run-to-run noise
findings.location: §5.10, "CV falls monotonically as the slow path becomes more common: 1.458 where there is no slow path at all, then 1.320, 1.254 and 1.243 as incidence rises" and "An operator watching CV would rank the workload containing no slow path as the most variable of the five"; acted on in §6.4 item 2, "Do not substitute the coefficient of variation for it".
findings.problem: The reversed-ordering result is presented as a property of the statistic, but every CV value comes from a single run per workload, and the gap that produces the headline rank (cheap 1.458 vs 0.1% mix 1.320) is driven entirely by that run's mean, which varies more than the gap across the workload's own repeats.
findings.evidence: results/mixed/percentile_ladder.json was computed from run2 of each workload only: its n values (e.g. uniform_cheap n = 2,431,591) match only the run2 rows of results/mixed/index.csv, and only the run2 directories contain requests.csv. In index.csv the three non-warmup uniform_cheap runs have means 0.3369, 0.3708 and 0.3738 ms, while the 0.1% mix run2 mean is 0.3785 ms, with near-identical distributions otherwise (p90 1.0031 vs 1.0038, p99 1.5062 vs 1.5064, p50 0 for both). Since CV = std/mean with a shared std near 0.49-0.50 ms, runs 3 and 4 of the cheap workload would give CV near 1.32-1.35, i.e. level with the 0.1% mix rather than above it. The 1% vs 10% gap (1.254 vs 1.243, 0.9%) is smaller still.
findings.fix: State in §5.10 that only run2 of each workload has a per-request series and that the cheap workload's mean varied by 11% across its three retained runs, which is larger than the CV gap being interpreted. Keep only the separation that survives that spread (workloads with 1% or less slow path score about 1.25-1.46; the all-expensive workload 0.31), drop "falls monotonically", and rewrite §6.4 item 2 as a caution about relative dispersion near the timer floor rather than a demonstrated ranking failure.

findings.title: H1 refuted, and "garbage collection keeps pace indefinitely", from a single one-hour run at one concurrency on one route
findings.location: §5.4, "One continuous run of 3,599 seconds at the knee" then "There is no sustained degradation (Fig. 5). H1 is refuted." and "The per-request cost is real, but it does not accumulate. The mechanism is expensive and stateless: each request allocates and releases, and garbage collection keeps pace indefinitely."
findings.problem: A hypothesis about behaviour under sustained load is declared refuted on n = 1, at one concurrency level on one route, and the absence of memory growth over one hour is extended to an unbounded claim. The repeat-count disclosure in §7 omits this arm entirely, so a reader cannot see that it is a single run.
findings.evidence: paper/facts.json records the soak as one run (soak_requests 4,221,421, soak_span_s 3,599; provenance results/soak/metrics.json), and unlike the matrix and mixed arms there is no per-run index file for it. §7 "Repeat counts" gives n for Arms A, B, C, D and E but never for the soak, nor for the calibration sweep, which docs/calibration.md records as "ten constant-VU runs, 20 s each", i.e. one run per level - yet §6.2 and the abstract quote its p99/p50 peak of 3.85 at 4 VUs against 3.47 at 8 VUs, a 10% difference from unreplicated 20 s runs. "Indefinitely" rests on four quarter-means, 242.8 / 245.2 / 246.7 / 246.4 MB (soak_rss_quarters), which still rise slightly across the first three quarters.
findings.fix: Add the soak (n = 1) and the calibration sweep (n = 1 per level) to the §7 "Repeat counts" paragraph and state the soak's n in §5.4. Downgrade to what one run supports: "no degradation was observed over 3,599 s in a single run at the knee" rather than "H1 is refuted", and replace "garbage collection keeps pace indefinitely" with "garbage collection kept pace for the hour observed; longer runs would be needed to exclude slow accumulation." Note in §6.2 that the exact location of the divergence peak (4 vs 8 VUs) is not replicated, only the decline beyond it.

findings.title: Findings from one loopback application with no database and no network are stated as facts about production systems
findings.location: §5.1, "Percentile analysis adds most information near the onset of saturation, which is where production systems normally sit"; §6.1, "That condition ... also describes most real degradations: a slow dependency on one code path, a cache-miss class, a tail of large records."
findings.problem: Both sentences are empirical claims about populations - production systems generally, and real degradations generally - that the study never sampled. It observed one application, one runtime, one host, on loopback, with one injected variance mechanism.
findings.evidence: §3 states the subject is a single hand-written Node.js server for which "There is no database"; §4.1 gives the target as "http://127.0.0.1:8099, loopback only" on a host shared with the generator; §7 concedes "Absolute latencies contain no network component" and "One Node.js server with one degradation mechanism." Every provenance path in paper/facts.json points to this study's own results/ directories - there is no production telemetry anywhere in the data. None of the three examples in §6.1 was tested: Arm C induced variance by mixing /robots.txt with /api/content (§5.6, and results/mixed/index.csv mix columns "90:/robots.txt,10:/api/content").
findings.fix: Mark both as conjecture tied to the mechanism rather than to a population. §5.1: "Percentile analysis added most information near the onset of saturation in this system; whether production systems typically operate in that region was not measured here." §6.1: "The same condition would be expected wherever cost is concentrated in a minority of requests - a slow dependency on one code path, a cache-miss class, a tail of large records - though only one such construction was tested."

findings.title: Novelty and gap claims about the literature are asserted without a search, and a textbook queueing result is framed as counter-intuitive
findings.location: §1, "It is rarely tested on a single system where the cause of degradation is known and can be varied deliberately"; §2 Gap, "The practitioner literature argues for percentiles largely from first principles and from observational data on production systems, where the cause of any degradation is not controlled"; §1.2 contribution 2, "That reverses the intuition that percentiles matter most when a system is most stressed."
findings.problem: "Rarely tested" and "largely from first principles" are claims about the state of a literature, made with no search strategy, screening record or count behind them. Contribution 2 claims to reverse an intuition for an effect the paper itself derives from Little's Law and calls obvious.
findings.evidence: docs/decision_log.md mentions a literature review only in passing (D17, "Arm E added: coordinated-omission control (found during the literature review)"); no search strategy, source list, date range or screening record exists in docs/, and the paper cites eleven works with no survey. Cited reference [6], Schroeder, Wierman and Harchol-Balter, contradicts the gap claim - §2 itself says they "establish the same point experimentally, showing that open and closed workload models produce substantially different behaviour in real systems." The paper also undercuts contribution 2: §5.1 calls the effect "Little's Law with throughput pinned" and §6.2 calls it "counter-intuitive, and mechanically obvious in hindsight".
findings.fix: Replace the unsupported quantifiers with what can be shown - "No controlled single-system decomposition of this kind was found among the sources reviewed here" - and name those sources. Reword contribution 2 to claim the measurement rather than the novelty: "A quantification, on one system, of how tail divergence varies with load: p99/p50 peaks near the saturation knee and falls under heavy queueing, as post-saturation queueing predicts but as percentile-monitoring advice rarely notes."

findings.title: §6.4 justifies its main recommendation with a statement its own data contradicts: absolute divergence grows under load, it does not shrink
findings.location: §6.4 Implications for practice, item 2: "Prefer a ratio of percentiles, p99/p50, over absolute percentiles when watching for emerging problems, since absolute divergence shrinks under heavy load."
findings.problem: The reason clause is backwards. Every arm in §5 shows absolute divergence rising with load; it is the RELATIVE divergence (the p99/p50 ratio) that shrinks. As written, the recommendation to prefer a ratio rests on a premise the paper elsewhere refutes.
findings.evidence: Computed p99 minus p50 from the §5.1 calibration values (facts.json calib_p50_* / calib_p99_*): 1.72-0.89 = 0.83 ms at 1 VU, 1.46 at 2, 5.80 at 4, 9.36 at 8, 10.38 at 16, and 109.93-94.35 = 15.58 ms at 200 VUs — monotonically INCREASING. Arm D is the same: p99-mean = 10.04, 19.26, 68.26, 710.33 ms across x1 to x1000 (facts.json scaled_*_p99 / scaled_*_mean). The paper says so itself in two other places: the Fig. 4 caption, "Absolute latency rises with load while the tail becomes relatively less extreme", and §6.2, "the distribution tightens in relative terms". docs/calibration.md states it explicitly: "Absolute p99 keeps rising, but the tail stops being *distinctively* worse than the median."
findings.fix: Replace "since absolute divergence shrinks under heavy load" with "since relative divergence shrinks under heavy load while absolute latency rises, so an absolute percentile threshold fires late" (or wording to that effect).

findings.title: §5.1 reports the 200-VU peak throughput as the post-saturation plateau, contradicting the calibration sweep it is describing
findings.location: §5.1, "Beyond that point the server delivers approximately 2,116 requests per second regardless of client count"
findings.problem: 2,116 req/s is the single highest value in the sweep, measured at 200 VUs. It is not the plateau rate "beyond" 8 VUs, and the sentence directly precedes a claim of throughput invariance that the sweep's own 8- and 16-VU rows falsify.
findings.evidence: The substituted fact is keyed calib_peak_rps = 2116 in paper/facts.json (provenance: results/calibration/sweep.csv), i.e. the peak, not a plateau. The sweep in docs/calibration.md gives req/s of 1951 at 8 VUs, 1917 at 16, 1946 at 32, 2020 at 64, 2076 at 100, 2075 at 150, 2116 at 200 — the 8- and 16-VU levels are 7.8% and 9.4% below 2,116. The same working note states the correct figure: "Past 8 VUs the server delivers ~1,950-2,100 req/s no matter how many clients wait." The paper's own §5.2 Arm A table also shows 1,174 to 2,269 req/s at these levels.
findings.fix: Substitute a plateau range rather than the peak — e.g. "delivers approximately 1,950 to 2,100 requests per second regardless of client count" — and add a facts.json key for the plateau instead of reusing calib_peak_rps.

findings.title: §6.1 attributes to the soak arm a result the soak arm does not contain
findings.location: §6.1, "Where cost rises uniformly, whether through deeper queues (§5.1), larger datasets (§5.5) or sustained load (§5.4), the mean tracks the change faithfully and the ratio of p99 to mean falls."
findings.problem: Neither half of the claim holds for §5.4. The soak varied nothing but time and found no change for the mean to track, and it is a single condition, so no ratio can rise or fall within it. Only §5.5 actually reports a falling p99/mean; §5.1 reports p99/p50, a different ratio.
findings.evidence: §5.4 states "There is no sustained degradation (Fig. 5). H1 is refuted", with a degradation ratio of 0.9944 (facts.json soak_degradation) and effect size r = 0.0417. The §5.4 table reports mean, p50/p95/p99/p99.9, early/late p95, p and r — no p99/mean ratio at any point, and no second condition to compare against (facts.json holds a single soak_ratio = 2.56, which the paper never prints). The falling p99/mean, 2.55 to 1.13, comes only from Arm D (scaled_x1_api_content_ratio / scaled_x1000_api_content_ratio). The §5.1 table is captioned "Tail divergence (p99/p50)".
findings.fix: Split the sentence: cite §5.1 and §5.5 for the falling divergence ratio (naming p99/p50 for §5.1 and p99/mean for §5.5), and cite §5.4 separately for the distinct finding that uniform per-request cost does not accumulate over time.

findings.title: §4.2 and Appendix A claim every number is machine-substituted; many numbers are literal text in the template and absent from facts.json
findings.location: §4.2, "Every number in this paper is generated by substitution from a machine-collected fact file derived from run outputs; none is transcribed by hand"; Appendix A, "Every numeric claim in this paper was substituted from `paper/facts.json`, which records the source file for each value."
findings.problem: Both statements are false as written. A line-by-line comparison of paper_template.md with paper.md shows a substantial set of numeric claims that the build never touched — they are hand-typed constants with no entry in facts.json and therefore no recorded provenance.
findings.evidence: Lines identical in paper_template.md and paper.md (i.e. containing no {{placeholder}}) include: "982 lines", "22 static HTML pages", "38 MB of static assets" (§3); "seventeen metric points per request" and "116.8 MB" (§4.2); "+35% (1->2) through +21% (2->4) and +10% (4->8) to -2% at 16 VUs" (§5.1); "n = 4 per cell" (§5.2 and §7); "12,000 offered requests per second", "4,000 virtual users", "2.0 s" (§5.3); "110 bytes", "87 KB", "120 s" (§5.6); "174 searchable records" (§5.7); and the whole `records` column of the Arm D table (188 / 1,880 / 18,800 / 188,000). I searched facts.json (271 keys): none of the values 982, 174, 38, 22 or 116.8 appears, and there is no key for the per-doubling throughput gains or the per-cell n. The underlying figures are correct against source (docs/environment.md line 31 and 67, docs/sut.md line 319), but they were transcribed, not substituted.
findings.fix: Either add these to collect_facts.py so they are genuinely substituted with provenance, or soften both sentences to their true scope, e.g. "Every measured result in this paper is generated by substitution from a machine-collected fact file; fixed properties of the application and test configuration are stated from the design record in docs/."

findings.title: The paper says six arms; the §4.5 table lists eight and §5 reports eight
findings.location: Abstract, "under six controlled load arms"; §4.5 table caption, "The six experimental arms and the variable each isolates."
findings.problem: The table sitting directly under that caption has a column headed "Arm" with eight rows, and §5 gives each of those eight its own results subsection. No reading of the table yields six.
findings.evidence: The §4.5 table rows are: Calibration; A, load matrix; Stress; Soak; D, dataset scale; C, variance injection; B, rate limiting; E, open-loop control — eight. §5.1 through §5.8 report exactly those eight in the same order. The figure caption immediately below the table, "Five arms vary uniform cost; only Arm C varies its distribution", sums to six only by excluding Arm B and Arm E, which the table itself lists as arms. (FINDINGS.md line 19 carries the same "Six controlled arms" wording, so the count is inherited rather than introduced here.)
findings.fix: Change both to "eight", or introduce a stated distinction — e.g. "six load arms plus a calibration sweep and a coordinated-omission control" — and make the Fig. 2 caption's count consistent with whichever convention is chosen.

findings.title: The "time-quantized percentile" measures within-second averaging, not sampling bias — the study's own data show the rate-weighting bias is ~0.007 ms, not 10.176 ms
findings.location: §4.3 "Each run therefore also reports a percentile computed over per-second means, and the gap between the two is reported as the sampling bias"; §5.9 table row "soak (3600 s, 8 VUs) | 17.436 ms | 7.26 ms | 10.176 ms" and "The bias is large, over half the reported value in the soak case"; §1.2 contribution 4 "a measurement of percentile sampling bias arising from time-varying request rates"; §6.4 item 3
findings.problem: The stated mechanism is that fast periods emit more requests, so raw percentiles over-represent healthy behaviour. The implemented statistic (`quantized_series` in scripts/analyze_k6.py, then `np.percentile(q, 99)`) computes the p99 of per-second MEANS. Averaging within each second destroys almost all within-second dispersion, so p99(per-second means) is far below p99(raw) even when the request rate is perfectly constant. The 10.176 ms gap is that averaging artefact, not rate-weighting bias, and the paper's conclusion that "a percentile is therefore not one well-defined quantity" is drawn from a statistic that does not measure what it is said to measure.
findings.evidence: I recomputed from results/soak/requests.csv (4,221,421 rows, reproducing raw p99 = 17.436 and quantized p99 = 7.260 exactly, matching results/soak/metrics.json). The actual correction for the stated bias — weighting each request by 1/(requests in its 1 s interval) — gives a rate-weighted p99 of 17.443 ms against a raw 17.436 ms, i.e. the raw figure is optimistic by 0.007 ms, not 10.176 ms. The mean of per-second p99s is 17.399 ms. Per-second request counts are nearly constant (min 857, max 1223, mean 1173, CV = 0.021), so there is almost no over-representation to correct. Same result on results/smoke/requests.csv: raw p99 1.888, rate-weighted 1.891, mean of per-second p99s 1.852, per-second count CV = 0.031 — against the paper's claimed 0.847 ms bias.
findings.fix: Replace the estimator with one that actually reweights by time: either a rate-weighted percentile over raw samples (weight = 1/count-in-interval) or a summary across per-second p99s. Both give a measured bias of roughly 0.01–0.05 ms here. Then rewrite §5.9 to report that the closed-loop design held the arrival rate nearly constant (per-second count CV ≈ 2%) so percentile sampling bias was negligible; withdraw contribution 4 in §1.2 and recommendation 3's sampling-unit clause in §6.4, or restate them as the trivially arithmetic observation that a percentile of per-interval averages is a different and much smaller quantity.

findings.title: Arm C's percentile ladder and the entire CV result rest on one arbitrarily selected run out of four, and the discarded runs contradict values printed in the paper
findings.location: §5.6 "Percentiles below are computed over the full per-request series of a single 120 s run per workload (n given), not from aggregated summaries"; Arm C ladder table row "99 / 1 mix | 1,918,671 | 0.446 | 0.000 | 1.006 | ..."; §5.10 table and "CV falls monotonically as the slow path becomes more common: 1.458 ... down to 0.312"
findings.problem: Four runs of each Arm C workload were executed (results/mixed/index.csv) but per-request data was retained only for run 2, and every ladder and CV number in the paper is that single run. The other retained runs disagree materially, including on a value the paper prints, and the §5.10 CV ordering — the paper's headline that the workload with no slow path is ranked most variable — is not shown to be stable against that run-to-run variation.
findings.evidence: results/mixed/index.csv: for mix_1pct, run 2 (the one used) gives p50 = 0.0 and p95 = 1.5039, while runs 3 and 4 give p50 = 0.5165 / 0.5162 and p95 = 1.0267 / 1.0246. The paper's ladder prints p50 = 0.000 for the 99/1 mix; three of four runs contradict it. For uniform_cheap the mean moves 0.3369 (run 2, used) → 0.3708 → 0.3738 across retained runs, an 11% swing, and CV = std/mean falls as the mean rises. Fitting the two-point 0-vs-~0.94 ms structure I measured in results/mixed/uniform_cheap_run2/requests.csv (64.2% of samples exactly 0, mean of non-zero 0.9407), that 11% mean swing corresponds to a CV drop of ~0.107 within a single workload, against a total reported range across the four cheap-dominated workloads of only 1.458 − 1.243 = 0.215. Meanwhile mix_0p1pct's means run 0.3785 (used) → 0.3723 → 0.3700, which moves its CV in the opposite direction. Only run 2 of each has requests.csv, so the paper cannot show the ordering survives.
findings.fix: Re-run the extraction so per-request series are kept for all retained Arm C runs, then report each ladder and CV cell as mean ± range over n = 3, or state explicitly that a single run was analysed and give the between-run spread already recorded in results/mixed/index.csv (mean, p50, p95, p99 per run). If the CV ordering does not survive, §5.10 and the §6.4 recommendation against CV must be softened to "CV can invert" rather than "the workload containing no slow path scores highest".

findings.title: Mann-Whitney result is reported as p = 0, is attributed to the wrong sample size, and its independence assumption is violated without comment
findings.location: §5.4 table row "Mann-Whitney p | 0" and "The Mann-Whitney test returns p = 0, conventionally read as highly significant ... At 4.2 million samples any difference at all attains significance"
findings.problem: Three separate defects. (a) A p-value cannot be zero; 0.0 is a floating-point underflow of scipy's normal approximation and reporting it literally is indefensible. (b) The test was not run on 4.2 million samples — it compared the 600 s early and late windows only. (c) Response times from a closed-loop queueing system are strongly autocorrelated, so the Mann-Whitney U independence assumption fails and the nominal p is invalid irrespective of n; the paper's stated explanation (large n) is incomplete, which weakens the methodological lesson it draws.
findings.evidence: results/soak/metrics.json records mannwhitney_u = 237155788609.5 and mannwhitney_p = 0.0. Recomputing the early/late windows from results/soak/requests.csv gives n1 = 705,515 and n2 = 701,522 (total 1,407,037, not 4,221,421 — the soak_requests fact in paper/facts.json). From those, the normal-approximation z = −42.8 and log10(p) ≈ −400, i.e. p ≈ 1e-400, which underflows double precision to 0.0. The rank-biserial effect size itself checks out: analyze_k6.py computes 1 − 2U/(n1·n2) = 0.0417, matching soak_effect_r in facts.json.
findings.fix: Report "p < 1e-300 (normal-approximation z = −42.8; scipy underflows to 0)" in the table and text. Change "At 4.2 million samples" to "Across the 1.41 million samples in the two 600 s windows". Add one sentence noting that successive response times in a closed-loop test are autocorrelated, so the effective sample size is far below n and the nominal p-value is doubly uninterpretable — which strengthens rather than weakens the section's argument for effect sizes.

findings.title: The 2.43x coordinated-omission factor averages two runs that differ 3.5-fold, one of which shows essentially no bias, yet the paper draws a directional conclusion from it in two places
findings.location: §5.8 "the open model reports a p99 of 36.685 ms against 15.097 ms for the closed model, a factor of 2.43 ... coordinated omission is present and measurable"; §7 Closed-model measurement, "The bias direction is optimistic, meaning reported tail divergences are conservative"
findings.problem: The reported 36.685 ms is the mean of two retained runs whose p99s are 56.9385 ms and 16.4309 ms. The lower run is within 9% of the closed-model 15.097 ms, i.e. it shows no meaningful coordinated omission at all, and the reported point value corresponds to no observed run and exceeds two of the three runs executed. The §5.8 spread caution says the exact factor should not be quoted precisely, but §5.8 and §7 both go on to assert the bias is "present and measurable" and that all reported tail divergences are therefore conservative — a claim n = 2 with a 3.5-fold internal disagreement cannot carry.
findings.evidence: results/open/index.csv, target_rate 1100: run 1 (warm-up, discarded) p99 = 21.5688, run 2 p99 = 56.9385, run 3 p99 = 16.4309. Mean of runs 2 and 3 = 36.685, matching arme_1100_p99 in paper/facts.json. Closed-model comparator is arma_api_content_v8_p99 = 15.097 (results/matrix/aggregate.json, p99_ms_sd = 0.076 over n = 4). So the closed-model figure is stable to ±0.5% while the open-model figure it is being divided into varies by a factor of 3.5 between two runs.
findings.fix: Print the two per-run p99s (16.4 and 56.9 ms) in the Arm E table rather than only their mean, and state the bias as a range (1.1x to 3.8x) rather than "a factor of 2.43". Downgrade the §5.8 and §7 conclusions to "consistent in direction but not quantified", or add runs at 1100/s until the p99 stabilises. The saturation-cliff result at 1400/s is unaffected — all three runs there agree closely (p99 2751.8 / 2771.8 / 2698.2) and should carry the section's argument instead.

findings.title: No dispersion measure is reported for any comparison, and the percentile estimator used in the Arm A and Arm D tables is never stated
findings.location: §7 Repeat counts, "The effects reported are large relative to the observed spread"; Arm A table (§5.2) and Arm D table (§5.5); §4.3 "Percentiles are reported at p50, p95, p99 and p99.9"
findings.problem: The paper prints no standard deviation, range or confidence interval for any multi-run cell, so the §7 claim that effects are large relative to the observed spread is unverifiable from the paper itself. Separately, the Arm A and Arm D percentiles are means of per-run percentiles, not percentiles of the pooled per-request series — a different estimator, and the only place the paper hints at the distinction is §5.6's aside that Arm C's figures are "not from aggregated summaries". The soak's degradation ratio (0.9944), on which H1's refutation rests, is a single run with no interval attached.
findings.evidence: scripts/aggregate.py builds each cell from `vals.mean()` over per-run p50/p95/p99 columns and writes `p99_ms_mean`, which collect_facts.py carries into paper/facts.json (e.g. arma_api_content_v8_p99 = 15.097 = mean of four per-run p99s). The spreads already exist and are never printed: results/matrix/aggregate.json gives p99_ms_sd = 0.0762 for that cell, and results/scaled_merged/aggregate.json gives x1000 p99_ms_sd = 107.48 (min 6031.60, max 6183.60) from only 363 requests across two runs. Grepping paper/paper.md for confidence/interval/±/sd returns only the §5.8 spread caution and the within-run std column of the §5.10 CV table.
findings.fix: Add a ± column (SD or min–max over retained runs) to the Arm A and Arm D tables, using the *_sd / *_min / *_max fields already in the aggregate JSONs. State in §4.3 that cell percentiles are the mean of per-run percentiles rather than percentiles of pooled samples. Attach an interval to the soak degradation ratio — a moving-block bootstrap on the early/late p95 ratio is the right tool here given the autocorrelation; a naive iid bootstrap on the retained windows already gives roughly [0.988, 1.000], which supports the no-degradation conclusion and is worth stating rather than leaving implicit.

findings.title: Arm C's "identical expensive work" premise is contradicted by the study's own per-request data: incidence is confounded with the cost of the slow path itself
findings.location: §5.6, "Identical expensive work is present in both; the mean reports it 4.4x more optimistically"; also Abstract, "diluting identical expensive work from 100% to 10% of requests"; also §5.6 bullet, "At 0.1% incidence, p99 is completely blind"
findings.problem: The arm's claim is that only the *distribution* of a fixed quantum of expensive work varies. In fact the per-request cost of /api/content changed by 3-6x across cells, and the absolute amount of expensive work changed too, so the independent variable was never isolated. The paper's caveat paragraph mentions self-queueing qualitatively but understates the magnitude, and the §5.6/§8/Abstract claims are stated as if the expensive work were held constant. Consequently the headline "invisible to p99" result is over-attributed to the rank-vs-incidence boundary: at 0.1% incidence there was, by measurement, almost no slow path present for p99 to miss.
findings.evidence: Counted directly from the retained per-request series. results/mixed/uniform_expensive_run2/requests.csv: 111,772 of 139,217 requests (80.3%) exceed 6 ms, and 139,214 of 139,217 (99.998%) exceed 3 ms. results/mixed/mix_0p1pct_run2/requests.csv: the mix ratio 999:1 implies ~2,224 requests hit /api/content, yet only 10 requests in the entire 2,224,121-request run exceed 6 ms and only 802 exceed 3 ms — fewer than the 0.041% over 3 ms in the pure-cheap run (percentile_ladder.json frac_over_3ms 0.0361 vs 0.0405). results/mixed/mix_1pct_run2/requests.csv: ~19,187 expensive requests, but only 63 exceed 6 ms and 8,781 exceed 3 ms. Volume also differs: results/mixed/index.csv gives uniform_expensive run2 = 139,217 expensive requests at 1,160 req/s, against mix_10pct run2 = 865,439 x 10% = 86,544 expensive requests at 721 req/s (62% of the work, 62% of the rate), and mix_0p1pct run2 = 18.5 expensive req/s, a 63x lower load on the very endpoint whose latency is being compared. Because mixed_load.js uses executor 'constant-vus' at 8 VUs, total offered load also floated from 1,160 to 20,263 req/s across cells — a 17.5x range that was never controlled.
findings.fix: Do not state that expensive work is identical across Arm C cells. Either (a) report the measured per-cell cost of the expensive endpoint (e.g. count of requests over 3 ms and over 6 ms, which the retained CSVs already support) and reframe the arm as varying incidence *and* slow-path severity together, or (b) re-run Arm C under a constant-arrival-rate executor with the expensive endpoint pinned to a fixed absolute rate (e.g. 100 expensive req/s in every cell) and the cheap endpoint varied to set incidence, so queue composition and expensive-arrival rate are held constant. At minimum, rewrite the §5.6 caveat to state the measured magnitude, and qualify the 0.1% invisibility claim: p99 was blind partly because the rank sits below the incidence and partly because the slow path was not slow in that condition.

findings.title: Arm B's limiter on/off contrast is perfectly confounded with session, server process instance, and run order, and one retained warm-up run inflates the baseline
findings.location: §5.7, "Nothing else differed between the two conditions; the limiter was switched by an environment variable. 6 runs were kept with it off and 2 with it on, in both cases after discarding a warm-up."
findings.problem: The two conditions were never interleaved or randomised. All limiter-ON runs were collected in one 4-minute block; the limiter-OFF runs were split across two sessions 9.5 hours apart, with the second batch collected the next night after Arm C had been running load for 40 minutes. Because the toggle is read from process.env inside applyRateLimit(), each condition necessarily ran on a different Node process, so process age and heap state are confounded with condition. Separately, the one-run warm-up discard did not remove the OFF condition's start transient, and the residual transient biases the comparison in the direction of the reported result.
findings.evidence: generated_at fields in results/armb: enabled/run1-3 = 2026-08-24T16:35:06, 16:37:10, 16:39:14. disabled/run1-3 = 2026-08-24T16:28:53, 16:30:57, 16:33:00; disabled/run4-7 = 2026-08-25T02:02:24, 02:04:28, 02:06:31, 02:08:35 — after the Arm C block (results/mixed timestamps 01:20:50 to 02:00:18). Warm-up leakage: disabled run1 (discarded) avg = 34.512 ms / 231.5 rps, run2 (retained) = 20.833 ms / 383.2 rps, run3 = 18.418 / 433.3, runs 4-7 = 18.159, 18.129, 18.113, 18.129 ms and 439.6-440.6 rps. The mean of retained runs 2-7 is exactly 18.63 ms and 429.5 rps, i.e. the paper's "18.63 ms" and "429 req/s" both include run2, which sits 15% above the stable value. Excluding runs 2 and 3 gives ~18.13 ms, moving the headline from 52.8x to ~51.4x and 46.9x to ~45.8x. The ON condition shows no equivalent transient (0.3520 / 0.3533 / 0.3528 ms across all three runs), so the bias is one-sided.
findings.fix: State in §5.7 that the conditions were run as separate blocks in different sessions and on different server process instances, and drop or qualify "Nothing else differed between the two conditions". Either re-run Arm B with the conditions alternated A/B/A/B within one session, or report the OFF condition using only the runs that had reached steady state (runs 3-7) and give the headline ratios to two significant figures with the spread. Note in §7 Threats that Arm B is a between-session comparison.

findings.title: The calibration sweep — the sole basis for the paper's second contribution — is unreplicated, monotonically ordered, and uniquely exempt from the warm-up discard applied everywhere else
findings.location: §5.1, "Divergence peaks at 4 VUs and then declines monotonically"; §1.2 Contribution 2, "tail divergence peaks near the onset of saturation and *decreases* under heavy load"; §5.1, "10 constant-VU levels from 1 to 200 virtual users were run for 20 s each"
findings.problem: Concurrency level is perfectly confounded with elapsed time since server start. The sweep runs one 20 s trial per level, in strictly increasing VU order, with only a 3 s settle, and — unlike Arm A, B, C, D and E — discards no warm-up run. The low-VU points that produce the divergence peak are therefore the first minute or so of load on the process, which is exactly the window the rest of the study treats as unusable. There is no replication, so no spread can be shown for the p99/p50 values that the paper's counter-intuitive claim rests on.
findings.evidence: scripts/calibrate.ps1: `[int[]]$Levels = @(1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 100, 150, 200)` iterated in a plain `foreach` with `Start-Sleep -Seconds 3`, writing one summary.json per level; results/calibration/sweep.csv contains exactly one row per level (no repeats). generated_at values run 12:57:03 (1 VU) through 13:00:35 (200 VU) on 2026-08-24, so the 1, 2 and 4 VU points are the first ~90 seconds of load after the 12:52:50 smoke run. By contrast scripts/run_matrix.ps1 marks `$warm = if ($run -eq 1) { "true" }` and the paper discards it everywhere; results/armb/disabled/run1.json shows the size of a first-run transient on this exact host — avg 34.512 ms against a steady 18.13 ms, 90% high. The 4 VU p99/p50 of 3.85 that anchors the claim is a single 20 s sample taken 47 seconds into the sweep.
findings.fix: Re-run the sweep with the level order randomised or counterbalanced, with a discarded warm-up run per level and at least n=3 replicates, and report the p99/p50 peak with its spread. If a re-run is not possible, state explicitly in §5.1 and §7 that the sweep is n=1 per level, ordered low-to-high without a warm-up discard, and downgrade Contribution 2 from "empirical evidence" to a single-sweep observation that Arm A's replicated matrix corroborates (Arm A p99/mean 4.63 at 2 VUs falling to 1.66 at 16 VUs is the replicated version of this claim and should carry the argument instead).

findings.title: The 2.43x coordinated-omission factor is the mean of two runs that disagree by 3.5x, one of which shows essentially no bias, and its closed-model comparator comes from a different session, duration and server process
findings.location: §5.8, "the open model reports a p99 of 36.685 ms against 15.097 ms for the closed model, a factor of 2.43. The closed-model percentiles used throughout this paper are therefore optimistic by roughly that factor"; §7, "The bias direction is optimistic, meaning reported tail divergences are conservative"
findings.problem: The number is not a measurement of a stable effect. It averages two retained runs whose p99 values differ by a factor of 3.5, and the lower of the two is statistically indistinguishable from the closed-model comparator — i.e. one of the two runs shows no coordinated-omission bias at all. The comparator itself is not a matched control: it was collected 12.5 hours earlier, in a different session, at a different run duration, on a server process that had been under load for over an hour, whereas Arm E restarts the server before its runs. The §5.8 spread caution acknowledges variance but the paper still propagates "roughly that factor" into §7 as a global correction on every tail divergence it reports.
findings.evidence: results/open/rate1100_run2/summary.json p99 = 56.938 ms; results/open/rate1100_run3/summary.json p99 = 16.431 ms; run1 (discarded warm-up) p99 = 21.569 ms. (56.938 + 16.431)/2 = 36.685, the paper's figure exactly. Run 3 alone gives 16.431 / 15.097 = 1.09x, no measurable bias. The closed comparator 15.097 ms is the Arm A /api/content 8-VU cell, generated_at 2026-08-24T14:08:16 to 14:20:30 at 180 s per run (run_matrix.ps1 default `$Duration = "180s"`), while the open runs are 2026-08-25T02:35:51 to 02:39:59 at 120 s (run_arm_e.ps1 `[string]$Duration = "120s"`) on a server just restarted by that script's Restart-Sut function. Arm A itself was never re-measured in the Arm E session.
findings.fix: Report the individual run values (16.4 and 56.9 ms) rather than only their mean, and state the factor as a range (1.1x to 3.8x) rather than "2.43". Add a matched closed-model control run inside the Arm E session, at the same 120 s duration and against the same freshly restarted process, so the open/closed contrast is within-session. In §7, replace "optimistic by roughly that factor" with a statement that the bias direction is consistent but its magnitude is not resolved at n=2, and stop propagating 2.43 as a correction factor. The §5.8 saturation-cliff result (n=3, all three 1400/s runs within 3%) is the robust part of this arm and should carry its weight.

findings.title: Arm C's percentile ladder and CV table come from whichever single run happened to retain raw output, and for the 1% mix that run disagrees with its three replicates
findings.location: §5.6, "Percentiles below are computed over the full per-request series of a single 120 s run per workload (n given), not from aggregated summaries"; §5.6 bullet, "At 1% incidence, p99 is at the boundary and barely separates (2.023 ms against 1.506 ms)"
findings.problem: Run selection was not random or pre-specified — it is run 2 in every workload, which is simply the run whose raw k6 output was kept on disk. For mix_1pct that run is visibly off its three siblings in the sub-millisecond region, and because the cheap-path latencies are quantised to a ~0.5 ms timer grid, statements of the form "identical" or "barely separates" can flip on which run is chosen. Neither the run-selection rule nor the disagreement between replicates is disclosed.
findings.evidence: Only the run2 directories under results/mixed contain requests.csv (mix_0p1pct_run2, mix_1pct_run2, mix_10pct_run2, uniform_cheap_run2, uniform_expensive_run2); runs 1, 3 and 4 hold summary.json only. results/mixed/index.csv for mix_1pct: run2 (the one used) p50 = 0, p95 = 1.5039; runs 1, 3 and 4 read p50 = 0.5166, 0.5165, 0.5162 and p95 = 1.0236, 1.0267, 1.0246. The grid is visible across the whole arm — p90 values cluster at 1.003-1.007 and p99 values at 1.5039-1.5064 — so the §5.6 claim that the 0.1% mix's p99 is "1.506 ms, identical to the pure-cheap workload's 1.506 ms" is an identity of timer buckets (1.5064 vs 1.5062), reported to four significant figures.
findings.fix: State in §5.6 which run supplied each ladder row and why, and add the p50/p95/p99 spread across the four replicates from index.csv so the reader can see mix_1pct's variation. Report the cheap-workload percentiles to the resolution the timer actually supports (e.g. "1.5 ms in both cases, one timer bucket apart") rather than to 1.506, and note the ~0.5 ms quantisation as a measurement constraint alongside the timer-floor discussion already in §5.10.
